#6757. How to Read the ‘Percy Jackson’ Books in Order of Release

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

With the new third season of Percy Jackson and the Olympians on Disney+, this is a great time to dive into Rick Riordan’s books, whether you’re reading them for the first time, rereading them, or picking up where you left off once upon a time. In true camp fashion, here’s your itinerary for reading all of the Percy Jackson books in order. (Or the Camp Half-Blood Chronicles, if you’d prefer to call them that.)

In the world that Riordan has created, demigods roam the Earth in modern times. For the most part, they’re indistinguishable from regular kids. Some of them, like Percy Jackson himself, don’t even know that their parents are literally figures from Greek and Roman mythology. Since there are so many of those centuries-old tales, Riordan has been able to turn them into a ton of young adult adventures.

In the first book, Percy Jackson learns that he’s a demigod and enrolls at Camp Half-Blood. He meets Annabeth Chase and Grover Underwood, and the three of them go on a quest to find Zeus’ lightning bolt.

This time, the teenage demigods go looking for the Golden Fleece. They’re joined by Tyson, Percy’s brother who happens to be a cyclops.

In the third book, which happens to be the basis for the current season of the Disney+ series, the group expands and they go on a rescue mission. For who exactly? You’re going to have to read to find out!

Camp Half-Blood is under attack (again), and our heroes enter the mythical Labyrinth to save it from invading forces.

In the (original) grand finale, the fight moves from Camp Half-Blood to Manhattan.

Fifteen years later, Riordan returned to his original hero with a duology about Percy’s last year in school. This means quests and college applications.

The final (unless there’s more) book is set at Halloween as he pet sits for Hecate. Should be easy!

But wait, there’s more! Riordan has dozens of other stories, long and short, in this universe. Here’s enough to get you started:

This is a series about a group of seven demigods who embark on a quest together.

This series is, like it says on the tin, about Apollo.

Nico also appears in Heroes of Olympus. This continues his story.

This series is set in the same universe, but all about Egyptian mythology.

These short stories are Percy Jackson and Kane sibling crossovers.

This trilogy is about Annabeth’s cousin and his dealings in Norse mythology.

The most recent book, co-written by Annabelle Oh, has a female protagonist: Katie Kim, daughter of Ares. It will get a sequel called The Rite of Aphrodite in March 2027.

#6756. GQ’s Best Gifts for Men 2026: 70+ Editor-Approved Presents

There's no shortage of stuff to buy for men. Stuff worth giving? That's another story. Fortunately, finding stuff worth giving is a salaried position around here. The results of that extensive retail research are all here: a carefully considered mix of great clothes, clever gadgets, handsome home goods, and a few things he probably wouldn't think to buy himself. We keep this guide updated throughout the year, so below you'll find our latest favorites alongside a few perennial heaters, all handpicked to make your gift-giving duties a little easier.

Still got names to cross off your list? Browse the rest of our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for a steady supply of good ideas.

This Banana Republic glen plaid double-breasted jacket features a rarely seen 2x1 button stance, which makes it a touch more casual but no less handsome.

Among Ralph Lauren's many contributions to American fashion is transforming the denim shirt from a Western novelty into a staple of the modern wardrobe. This weathered slub denim version is a handsome example, and something he'll wear for years to come.

Few knits occupy a place in the menswear pantheon quite like J.Crew's rollneck sweater. With its relaxed weave and raglan sleeves, it's an enduring heater that makes for an easy gift.

What makes Morjas' Belgian loafer so irresistible to those who've had the good fortune to wear it is just how comfortable it is. Doesn't hurt that it's also clean, understated, and versatile as all get-out.

Maple's Orbit bracelet is a great little way to add a fleck of personality to an otherwise understated fit. And if this design is a little too out-there for his taste, you may have to look elsewhere entirely. That's kind of Maple's whole thing.

Smaller, thinner cases are great, and the Timex Marlin is a stone-cold minimalist classic in that world. But it also sells out, so allow us to recommend another, newer Timex gem: the Marlin Jet Titanium. He'll love that it's an automatic, too.

Patagonia's Snap-T is an icon, and this new Re-Tool Air version gives it a fresh spin with an exclusive Polartec fleece that's remarkably lightweight, wonderfully warm, and made from 100% recycled polyester.

This merino wool crewneck from Arc'teryx is lightweight, great at regulating temperature, and just as good worn on its own as it is layered under a sweater or jacket. A go-to layering piece for just about any wardrobe.

If you ask us, the Moon Shoe is one of the Swoosh's best releases of the year. A perfectly retro, low-profile runner with a refreshingly affordable price tag.

A great hoodie is essential, and Reigning Champ nails fit-meets-function better than most, with an aesthetic inspired by old-school athletic training gear. This one is cut from the brand’s signature midweight terry, which is soft and substantial without feeling bulky.

A man can never have enough flannels. Filson's Rangeland is made from brushed 5.5-ounce cotton, and we're partial to the red and gray plaid.

Massachusetts-based Steele Canvas has been making sturdy canvas goods for generations, and its Everyday Tote is exactly the sort of gift they'll most definitely get some use out of.

When we think of field watches, we think of Hamilton. This no-nonsense mechanical number is hard to beat in the category, and you could spend a lot more on a lot less.

A good pair of cowboy boots can do wonders for a fit, and Tecovas' Warren makes a strong case for adding a little yee-haw to the rotation. With classic flame stitching and a sharp cutter toe, they're more versatile than you might think.

3sixteen's asymmetrical fleece is freaky, but not too freaky, with a wide boatneck, an off-center zipper at the neck, and an oversized pocket with a zip closure. There's a lot going on, but the proportions are spot-on.

Some of the best stuff Miansai makes is low-key its bead and stone jewelry. The Avi necklace is a welcome change of pace from the usual gold and silver.

John Smedley has been making knitwear in England for more than 200 years, and there's a reason it's still considered some of the best in the biz. This wool polo might look simple, but the quality of the knit, the fit, and the finishing make it something special.

OrSlow's 105 jeans have a classic straight leg and medium rise, with the kind of easy, timeless fit that never goes out of style. A very good upgrade for anyone whose denim rotation could use a little love.

Yes, it costs a pretty penny. But it also might be one of the coolest scarves we’ve ever seen: so robust you can wrap it around yourself a few times like a sweater, at which point the price starts to make more sense. Oh, and it’s Burberry.

Movado's iconic Museum Watch has been a masterclass in minimalism since 1947, with a Bauhaus-inspired dial that's blank save for a single dot at 12 o'clock. A remarkably sleek timepiece, especially at this price.

Some days call for a full wallet, others for just the essentials. Coach's 3-in-1 gives him both, with a removable ID insert that works just as well on its own when he wants to travel a little lighter.

For the record, we're all for giving socks as presents, provided they're of the same caliber as those from Japan's Rototo.

Quince is one of our first stops for affordable cashmere, but its merino wool offerings ain't too shabby either. Take this sweater, which it done up in cable-knit for a little somethin' somethin'.

Blundstone introduced its Heritage boot this year, a decidedly more upscale take on the brand's beloved Chelsea. Handmade from premium leather, it's also finished with a Goodyear welt that allows it to be resoled for years to come.

Come for the three iconic Byredo scents, which you can spritz according to whatever the mood calls for. Stay for the handsome leather case, which is almost reason enough to gift the set on its own.

Plenty of dopp kits come in sleek leather (no shade), and plenty of designer versions cost a small fortune (some shade). But most guys just want something that looks good and can take a beating on the road. Filson knows how to do that.

Bar soaps have officially entered the elevated grooming arena, with better ingredients and better scents. Made in France, this bar adds a pop of color by the tub, lathers like a dream, and carries Frama's gorgeous Herbarium aroma that lingers on skin long after the shower.

Bleu de Chanel's Parfum takes everything great about the original and turns it up a notch. Still zesty and botanical, but with sandalwood and tonka bean lending a richer, smoother finish.

Released this year, Braun's Nevo is arguably the best and most advanced foil shaver on the market today, and our own testing backs that up. Given the price tag, it's exactly the sort of splurge that makes for a great gift.

Vitamins B and C do wonders for the skin, and Aesop's B Triple C Facial Balancing Gel is packed with both. Deeply hydrating yet leaving a matte finish, it was a game changer when it debuted over 20 years ago, and it's still elite after all these years.

If he’s taking skincare cues from anyone, it should be Pharrell, who apparently doesn’t age. The multihyphenate’s skincare brand, Humanrace, has a Rejuvenating Face Mask featuring a peptide trio complex to keep your lucky guy looking chipper.

The Philips OneBlade 360 is a little groomer we love for its versatility. There’s really nothing quite like it out there, and it can handle just about any hairy situation.

Dior seems to drop a new olfactory banger every few months, and Bois d'Argent is one of the latest. Smooth woods, amber, and rich iris mingle with frankincense for a scent that's warm, elegant, and easy to wear just about anywhere.

Wonder Valley's newish Wild Garden hand wash puts olive oil to good use, whipping up a rich, softening lather with a cedar-and-herb scent that brings a little of the great outdoors to the sink.

A moisturizer is a no-brainer, but a serum signals one is getting extra serious about skincare. Caldera + Lab makes that addition easy: a few pumps deliver vitamin C, collagen amino acids, and skin-soothing botanicals to brighten, firm, and soften fine lines.

We've been longtime fans of Dr. Dennis Gross's Alpha Beta Universal Daily Peel pads, which make good skincare almost embarrassingly easy. A couple of swipes help exfoliate dead skin, smooth texture, and brighten the complexion.

Tower 28's travel-size SOS set packs everything they need to stay fresh on the go. A little skincare insurance for wherever the holidays take them.

Salt & Stone makes one of our favorite body washes, and this mini set lets them take the whole lineup for a spin.

With these hydrating eye patches from one of the best grooming brands to do it, no one will ever know he didn't get his proper eight hours last night.

You can buy all the fancy sunscreen you want, but convenience decides if you actually wear it. Freaks of Nature’s SPF 50 stick—small, glide-on, reef safe, and water-resistant for 80 minutes—nails it.

The LED mask market is booming, and Omnilux is at the top of the heap. This one is specifically designed and FDA-cleared for men’s typically thicker facial skin, targeting fine lines, firmness, and overall health, while helping calm any redness from shaving. In other words, it’s a Michael Myers-like mask that promises scary-good skin with consistency and patience.

Hair dryers have officially gotten techy-cool, and Laifen is a big part of it. The new SE 2 is so sleek and ergonomic, with intuitive controls to match, he'll want to leave it on display.

Smythson and Burberry joining forces is more British heritage than you can wave a Union Jack at. Smythson already makes a covetable travel chess set, but add Burberry's signature check and it's, well, checkmate.

ICYMI: Menswear's patron saint Todd Snyder linked up with West Elm for a stirring collection of homewares this past year, and the hands-down standout is this walnut valet chair. A handsome place to hang tomorrow's outfit—or yesterday's, if we're being realistic.

It's a tabletop lighter shaped like a mallard duck. Something you'd find in the study of a delightfully eccentric uncle, and exactly the sort of gift no one knows they want until they get one.

A speckled enamelware thermos from Polo Country, because why not.

Few brands have done more to make everyday essentials like bedding, towels, and sleepwear into objects of desire than Copenhagen's Tekla. Its PJs embody that sensibility: beautifully cut, made from crisp organic cotton, and available in a killer assortment colors and stripes.

I love this genre of slipper, the travel kind that zips into its own little case. And these from Luca come at an incredible price, with a perfectly shaped toe box and rubber soles that make them handsome enough to wear out.

If they're going to keep ordering pants off the internet, they might as well have a proper tool for opening all those packages. The Palmer knife makes short work of cardboard and packing tape, so they can get to the fit pics faster.

Hoto’s sleek PixelDrive electric screwdriver comes with 30 interchangeable bits and a nifty pixelated display that shows exactly how much power he’s working with. That wobbly dining chair doesn’t stand a chance.

This isn't one of those dinky makeup fridges. This is a countertop fridge fridge, the latest in beverage-holding innovation from Rocco. And of course, it looks great.

I picked up Nanu’s Arc earlier this year, and I’ve gotten way more joy out of it than I expected. It’s a well-built, thoughtfully engineered analog clock with a discreet digital display and a lovely mechanical chime. Not cheap, sure, but having one less reason to reach for my phone has been worth every penny.

Call me old-fashioned, but a man ought to know how to make a proper drink. And he ought to have the right tools for the job. Fellow's new eight-piece cocktail set has everything he needs to shake, stir, and strain his way to a good one.

It may come as a shock, but there's a whole world beyond burgers worth smashing. Caraway's immaculately designed grill press is up to the task.

A good set of bedsheets is a nice gift. An adult gift. It says, “I care about you, even when you're unconscious.” Parachute's brushed cotton sheets are those sheets: soft, cozy, and something they'll appreciate every single night.

Shinola's Michigan-made five-port power supply is a highly specific gift for the design obsessive in your life, but that's precisely why it'll hit.

Few things feel better than slipping into a plush robe at a fancy hotel, but honestly, most have nothing on Brooklinen's. Better yet, you don't need to spend $500 a night to get one.

Now that's one helluva coffee mug. Made from stainless steel with double-wall construction to keep it cool to the touch, this industrial number from Copenhagen-based design studio Service Projects comes with a generously proportioned saucer that does double duty as a serving tray.

John Waters warned against going home with someone who doesn't own books. I'd say the same rule goes for wine openers. And this one from Craighill really is the best.

You never know when you need a knife, pair of scissors, or a corkscrew—and now he'll never have to worry about missing any of those essential tools.

You could get him a candle. Or you could get him this handsome little contraption: a glass teardrop set in a brass cradle. Fill the glass with fragrance oil, light the tealight underneath, and voilà: instant home aura.

The most advanced vibe curators know: nothing sets the mood at home like well-crafted incense. Vyrao’s Verdant blend of bergamot, frankincense, and white musk packs a particularly calming punch as the seasons change.

Apple’s latest AirPods 3 refine a classic with noticeably better noise cancellation and a slick new live translation feature—proof the world’s best earbuds just keep getting smarter.

The new iPad mini gets its biggest glow-up yet, with a gorgeous 8.5-inch OLED display, the new A20 Pro chip, and a thinner, lighter build that's now water-resistant.

Some folks are organized, the rest of us have AirTags. The second-generation model improves the range, cranks up the speaker volume, and generally makes losing things less stressful.

Apple's brand-new HomeView brings the company's signature polish to the smart home, giving them a sleek new command center for everything from lights to thermostats.

Plenty of brands have tried their hand at recreating Sony's classic Walkman headphones, and now Sony itself is getting in on the action. The MDR-3R brings back that familiar retro look, this time with a USB-C connection.

In our nostalgia-addled times, people are buying iPods again. Fosi Audio's DAP Neo takes the idea and brings it into the present, with a familiar form factor, tactile scroll wheel, and the ability to play high-resolution lossless audio. This bundle comes with the brand's excellent wired earbuds.

Ray-Ban’s Audio Clubmasters pack open-ear audio and six built-in microphones into a classic frame. Best of all, he can enjoy the latest tech without making everyone wonder if they’re being filmed.

The new Beats 360 headphones sound great and look the part. Swappable performance-knit cushions let you customize the look, while a sweat- and water-resistance rating makes them a rare pair of gym-worthy over-ears.

Amazon's Kindle Colorsoft makes a pretty convincing case for a color e-reader: admire the illustrations in a Taschen book, give comic books and graphic novels their due, or finally get around to reading The Creative Act. It does that, too.

We’ll always have a soft spot for a pen and spiral pad, but the Paper Pro Move is for the serious note taker—sleek, responsive, and slim enough to slip in a jacket pocket.

There's a newer Ace Ultra on the scene, but we're still big fans of the original Sonos Ace. The sound is rich and full, the battery lasts forever, and they have that luxe, comfortable-yet-minimalist feel you'd expect from one of the best home-audio brands, period.

Sometimes you just need a speaker small enough to toss in a tote for park hangs, solo listening sessions, or an impromptu dance party. Marshall's Emberton III is a great option.

The Switch 2 was one of last year's biggest launches, but 2026 might be an even better time to gift one. With a growing library of excellent games and plenty of people still waiting to upgrade, it's a gift that's only gotten better with time.

Five generations in, JBL still hasn't found a reason to make the Go any bigger. And why would it? The pint-sized speaker continues to deliver outsized sound, with the latest iteration adding 10 hours of battery life and USB-C wired audio support. Still the one to beat in its size class.

Nocs Provisions is the first name in cool binoculars, and now it's got a lo-fi digital camera to match. It's a fun little shooter in its own right, but I love that you can take photos straight through a pair of binoculars or a monocular.

The future of tech is looking pretty darn analog. Polaroid’s newest instant camera makes is an interesting hybrid, with built-in creative modes and the singular pleasure of a photograph you can actually hold.

One of Nike ACG's most head-turning releases of the year, the Radical AirFlow shirt is a very good gift for the runner in your life, with a wild-looking, ultra-breathable fabric that'll make him look as cool as he feels.

We've been big fans of Bose's open-ear earbuds for a while now, and this sportier take is a good match for anyone who likes to break a sweat. All the great sound, while being easier on the ear canals.

The screenless fitness tracker category has really heated up this year, but Google's Fitbit Air is a standout. It tracks heart rate, sleep quality, blood oxygen, and workouts, with automatic activity detection and up to a week of battery life—all for a benjamin.

Oura's fifth-gen ring is slimmer, lighter, and more comfortable than ever, with improved sensors for keeping tabs on sleep, recovery, and all the other things going on under the hood.

Aer's new Sports Duffel Max carries on the brand's tradition of making excellent gym bags, with plenty of room for a weekend warrior's gear and a clever pop-out divider that makes organizing equipment for just about any sport a snap.

Beat those sore muscles into submission so you can get back at it sooner rather than later.

Electrolytes have gotten awfully sophisticated lately. Freaks of Nature's zero-sugar powder goes beyond hydration, with a formula designed to support gut health and the skin barrier, too.

For the guy who can't start (or end) his day without getting a quick sweat sesh in, these shorts will keep him going rep after rep, set after set.

Calves barking after a vacation run? Worry no longer, thanks to these portable massage sleeves, which are great for those guys who never want to miss a run or a lift even if they're supposed to be taking time to rest.

You might think running requires little more than a pair of sneakers, but you'd be surprised. This vest from Lululemon has pockets aplenty for all the little things he needs to bring along, without weighing him down.

Give the guy an excuse to take a load off. Lookout & Wonderland’s Magic Bath combines mineral-rich Japanese sea salt, French green clay, and nourishing oils with 500 mg of CBD for a seriously luxurious soak.

Any who has ever hit a squat rack, deadlifted, or run a mile, should grace their legs with the JetBoots Prime. In one of our editor's epic pursuit of tree trunk-sized quads, he's loved the way that these help reduce his recovery time and boosted his efficiency for his next leg day workout. Plus, they're ready to go on the road because they fold down so small.

Bowflex’s SelectTech dumbbells are about as functional as fitness equipment gets. A quick turn of the dial adjusts the weight, replacing an entire rack of dumbbells without turning his place into an Equinox.

The new Nike x Hyperice Air Zoom HyperSlide delivers targeted heat and vibration massage across the top of the foot, giving his hardworking dogs some well-earned R&R, rest day or not.

#6745. The Luxury Business of Las Vegas F1 Is Booming

If Formula 1 circuits were Mario Kart race tracks, the Las Vegas Grand Prix is as spiritually close to Rainbow Road as it gets.

This year, newly hybrid-engined F1 cars zoomed along an LED-lit Vegas Strip that had been closed off to civilian traffic each night of the event, much to the chagrin of every ride-share driver and/or tourist trying to cross Las Vegas Boulevard. They whipped past the Paris hotel casino’s glittering facsimile of the Eiffel Tower and the cartoonishly massive Sphere. They skirted under banners advertising Louis Vuitton and Qatar Airways. At the end, winner Max Verstappen was driven in a racing-striped stretch limousine, operated by a dashingly bedraggled Keanu Reeves, to the Fountains of Bellagio—inspired, like so many Vegas landmarks, by the architectural grandeur of Europe.

Max Verstappen, shortly after his win on Saturday night.

Motorsports enthusiast Keanu Reeves, center, drove the winners in a limo.

Since the Vegas GP was first revived in 2023, it has been a polarizing stop on the globe-trotting F1 calendar. (Back then, Verstappen called it “99 percent show and 1 percent sporting event.”) Even for a multibillion-dollar sport, was this too much glitz? Surrounded by sandy desert and snow-capped mountains, the gaudiest track in Formula 1 is nevertheless a sight to behold—and this year, it produced one of the most thrilling races in recent memory. Plus, as far as metropolises go, there are certainly more boring places to spend a few days than Sin City.

The winners’ podium: Red Bull’s Verstappen in first, followed by McLaren pair Lando Norris, left, and Oscar Piastri.

Well, unless you’re Kimi Antonelli, F1’s baby-faced world champ.

“The thing I like the most here is the track, because I’m not allowed to do anything else other than drive around,” Antonelli told me, with a smirk, ahead of the race last week. “Because I’m not 21.”

(The Italian, who turned 20 in August, became Formula 1’s youngest-ever world champion at the Mexico Grand Prix earlier this month. In Vegas, he and his Mercedes teammate George Russell just missed the podium, finishing fourth and ninth respectively after more than a few late-race heartbreaks.)

Mercedes drivers Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

But if you’re too old to wait in the line outside Marquee, there were plenty of other desirable libations afoot. Vegas has always been a place where fine cuisine (or at least, high-roller cuisine) means bumping up prices by dumping truffles and caviar on everything. The OG greats of modern dining—the Jean-Georges Vongerichtens and Wolfgang Pucks—have been here since the ’90s. But since COVID, a new generation of big-brass restaurateurs have set up shop on the Strip: Carbone Riviera and the Corner Store at the Bellagio’s properties; Sartiano’s and Delilah at the Wynn; Mother Wolf and Contramar at the Fontainebleau. (There are elite members’ clubs, too: Zero Bond opened at the Wynn in March.)

Brunch at Sadelle's, a popular Major Food Group spot, inside the Bellagio.

During Friday’s qualifying run, former F1 star Daniel Ricciardo stopped by the Corner Store at the Cosmopolitan, a wood-paneled outpost of the New York hotspot that opened a few weeks earlier. In the moody, multi-room space, the kitchen sends out platters of dry-aged wagyu and pepperoni pizza rolls while bartenders shake up sour-cream-and-onion martinis served with potato-chip sidecars. (The cocktail is purportedly Taylor Swift’s favorite, though executive chef Michael Vignola will neither confirm nor deny this: “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” said Vignola, grinning. “You can also ask Travis.”)

A day earlier, Ricciardo—who retired from F1 last year but came to town for a self-branded clothing pop-up and bar at the Bellagio—reflected on his own experience at the first-reprised Vegas GP in 2023. “It feels like a video game,” he said. “Whether the track is your favorite or not your favorite in terms of the actual layout, it’s still pretty surreal to be here and be the main event in a city that revolves around entertainment.”

According to Vignola, Ricciardo is a big fan of the Corner Store’s steak program as well as the chicken paillard, “a sleeper on the menu and a great mid-course this year.” Manning the kitchen at the Corner Store in Vegas, which has 100 more seats than the original NYC location, the chef said they’re selling about as much caviar here as they do in Manhattan.

“Because of the volume here, we are slightly selling a little bit more caviar, slightly, you know, maybe 2 to 1,” Vignola said with a laugh. Lately, they’ve started R&D’ing some Norwegian king crab legs, including a prototype for a “crab appletini.” They’re leaning into menu items that the New York-born chef described as “a little bit more Vegas, flashy kind of bespoke things. There are some high-roller dishes that pop off.”

An Elvis impersonator at F1's Paddock Club.

The likes of Vignola and Mario Carbone, as well as the actual Wolfgang Puck and Jean-Georges, hosted caviar-filled pop-up stands at the Bellagio Fountain Club suites during the F1 festivities. The starriest celebrities, including Reeves and Kim Kardashian, who’s dating driver Lewis Hamilton, watched the big race from the paddock, with a good view of the Elvis impersonator and humanoid robots who roamed the asphalt.

Over my few days in Vegas, multiple locals—including chefs, service and casino employees, and Uber and Lyft drivers—described how the city’s changed over the last 15 years. On the ride from the airport, my driver pointed to a new landmark on the horizon: a massive mirrored edifice shaped like the body of a guitar (the new Hard Rock Las Vegas hotel) that’s in the midst of being erected from the sand.

“I think Vegas and Formula 1, they were meant for each other,” said José Andrés, the Spanish-born chef who opened his first Las Vegas restaurants inside the then-freshly built Cosmopolitan in 2010. “I came here three weeks before the casino opened. And just to watch a casino open is the closest thing to watching a little egg hatch, or my daughter [being] born. For me to watch an entire casino from nothing to becoming a tower, it brings good memories.”

One can only imagine how we’ll look back on the Las Vegas Grand Prix—only in its fourth year—a decade or two from now, when all the cars are self-driving and the Strip has been converted into an actual rainbow speedway floating in deep space. Will there still be Champagne?

#6738. 17 Best Beard Trimmer Picks, Tested by GQ Editors in 2026

Every guy needs the best beard trimmer for his situation. Whether he grows it patchy, keeps it perma-stubbled, or is as lustrous as the A-List beards, a trimmer is mandatory in every beard kit. And not all beard trimmers are alike, which is why the best one for your facial hair style may be different from the next guy’s.

I tested a bunch of beard trimmers to deliver you a real who’s who of men’s grooming devices. This list reflects a range of options—some multitaskers, some detailers; some top-shelf, some a better buy for lower budgets. Above all, though, I ask you this: Make sure that the device you choose allows your beard to reach its full potential. That doesn’t mean you need a big bushy beard, but rather, you should be able to achieve whichever style (or a suite of styles) you want to wear over the next few years—which is the minimum amount of time any of these devices should last. Ideally, they’ll hum on for five to 10 years, anyhow.

Here are the best beard trimmers after we tested pretty much every last one of them. (And while you’re at it, consider my rosters of other grooming tools, from razors and electric shavers, to manscapers and hair clippers.)

Black Friday is here, and the deals are hitting fast. For the biggest and swerviest markdowns, editor favorites, and elite-level shopping intel, keep it locked on our roundup of the best Black Friday deals and best Black Friday clothing deals.

No sense in burying the headline: Philips Norelco’s Multigroom 9000 Series is, hands down, the best beard trimmer you can buy. And that’s before factoring in how much more it can do than just keep your facial hair in check than other electric razors that are found in your everyday grooming kit. (It’s also recently been renamed the “All-in-One 9000” but answers to both names.) For the last 5 or 6 years, this has been my single go-to trimmer. Everything else is trying to dethrone it, and so far, no true contest has emerged. In terms of customization and power, this device checks all of the boxes.

It all starts with the beating heart: "The Multigroom does not compromise on power or battery life, and it's very intuitive to use," says Fellow Barber’s Head of Education Emily Clark. The battery life truly over-delivers: your mileage may vary since Philips Norelco only claims a (still impressive) six hours of charge, but I got a ridiculous 17 hours of consecutive runtime fresh out of the box, thanks to a lithium ion battery. Speaking of the box, there’s a lot in there, all of it useful. Between the small tooth-like detail attachment and foil shaving head, the Multigroom 9000 makes it easy to style and sculpt with precision. One trimmer even adjusts by tenths of a millimeter to help you get the perfect designer stubble, if that's your aim. And that’s just its beard trimming bona fides. The Multigroom 9000 is also a solid hair trimmer (shout out to that brawny motor and battery again) and body hair trimmer as well. Covering off for three products, and doing it well, suddenly makes the $90 price tag look like a deal.

Long-term testing notes: Wouldn’t you know it… I lost the beloved little shaver on this one recently. Heartbreak. (Yeah, I can test a new one, but I realize now how much of my love for it is pinned on that micro shaving attachment.) I stand by the fact that it’s the best on the market, but without that shaver, the window has opened for me to spend time with other devices, like the Braun below. Let this be a lesson: Don’t unpack your Philips Norelco all-in-one in a hotel room without carefully auditing every single piece when you pack it up again. Adam Hurly

"This trimmer is great! It comes with so many attachments to use for your trimming needs. The battery lasts a long time, i have yet to have to charge mine and i've had it for a few months now.

The trimmer is super quiet as well as very well made. It's all made up of metal, not plastic, and feels like it will last a long time. It's fairly lightweight and easy to handle when [using] it. It also comes with a small cleaning brush that makes cleaning it up a breeze!"

Given how much I love the Philips Norelco Multigroom 9000, it’s no surprise that the more affordable model, the Multigroom 5000, is my budget choice to keep things manscaped. It offers most of the same steel-bladed precision and customization benefits as its fancier family member, albeit in a less durable body (plastic instead of stainless steel) and half the battery life. Still, its a three-hour battery power beast that bests many beard trimmers twice the price. And the lighter plastic body is nice for travel. The Philips Norelco Multigroom 5000 is great for anyone on a budget, but it’s not “budget."

Whereas other lower-priced beard trimmers can’t handle precise detailing, the Multigroom 5000 includes a detail trimmer and nose trimmer, not to mention hair clipper and body trimmer guards for versatility. It does lack the shaving detailer and the body shaver (as does the in-between 7000 model), which is important to note if you want that level of customization and don’t otherwise own a detail shaver that you also rely upon for bare-faced stretches of facial real estate. For this reason, I find it a little less perfect across the board compared to the 9000, but the price-to-precision ratio is hard to match. And if you want a great value above all—and a straightforward beard trimmer—meet your optimal Multigroom, the 5000.

Long-term testing notes: Recently, I used the 5000 consistently, and got quite cozy with it. Sure, it lacked the key shaving features of the 9000, but I think this is truly the best value device in the game when you only want a trimmer. Terrific muscle, terrific customization, great endurance. Five stars for this one. Adam Hurly

"This Phillips/Norelco trimmer works great. It is very quiet, the battery life is pretty long and it does exactly what I need it to do. It comes with a lot of attachments - haven’t used them all, but the ones I have used worked just fine. This is a good quality trimmer."

Hatteker is a surprise of a buy—it’s that “out of left field” Amazon brand that most of us recognize by name, despite not knowing anyone who uses it. This all-in-one kit covers every kind of hair-trimming task, from lineups to sideburns to beards, eyebrows, and body hair. What's more, it's a hair-cutting machine for full beards and stubble alike with multiple plastic guards. I bought the tool with little expectations for quality and care, but was consistently surprised at how well it held its own compared to the more reputable brands.

This device won’t win any design awards and certainly hasn’t reinvented the wheel, but most consumers won’t care about that stuff; they want a good beard trimmer that meets all their grooming needs, and Hatteker’s checks all of those boxes. I do wish its detailing trimmer was a bit narrower, but that’s me minding some very fine details. It’s also not up to the same quality as, say, Philips, Andis, Braun, Wahl, etc, but it’s also not low quality either. For $40, you get your money’s worth, especially considering that LED battery display and vast range of trimming lengths and clipping attachments. It’s still a great option if you’re not looking to spend a lot, or if our other best value winner, the Philips Norelco Multigroom 5000 Series, is out of stock.

Long-term testing notes: Every time I bring this one out, I am amused by how surprisingly great it is. It goes to show that those Amazon reviews really are one of the most accurate depictions of value; I long wrote the brand off because of its non-image compared to the big names, but in terms of performance and return on spend, Hatteker really clears the bar. Granted, I’m not using most of these devices more than a few times a quarter (since by and large I stick with my own favorites or test new ones) but my Hatteker remains strong and sturdy and has endurance, some three years after I first acquired it. Adam Hurly

"The trimmer is easy to use and the charge lasts a very long time. I have not had to recharge since the initial charge after taking it out of the box, trimming bi-weekly. It is not heavy. It’s easy to handle. The adjustment guides stay where you select. I don’t worry about them shifting during use. Beard maintenance is an easy job with this.”

The All-in-One 7000 makes a convincing case for clearing some space in your bathroom cabinet. A body hair trimmer that comes replete with several beard-related attachments, its precision comb kept stubble neatly between 1-3mm without pulling or leaving stray hairs behind. Sure, a dedicated beard trimmer will do a more precise job, but there's plenty of substance to this device's delirious accessory count.

The slightly boxy handle feels reassuringly secure when I'm cleaving away at a couple of days' growth, while a textured grip makes it well-suited to comfortably swerving across my chest, underarms, and more sensitive areas. If you dig them out from the bottom of their box, the nose and ear attachments prove useful enough to earn their place in the kit too. Philips rates this kit for up to five hours between charges – handy given how often you'll be using the thing – and the waterproof construction makes cleanup straightforward.

My main gripe is one that always crops up when I test Philips, Braun, and other established grooming brands’ devices – the proprietary charging connection. You’ll need its supplied cable, even if your drawer is already overflowing with USB-C leads. Still, for someone who wants to maintain short facial hair and keep the rest of their grooming in order with one tool, the 7000 covers a lot of ground. Esat Dedezade

“It's comfortable and quiet with an easy-to-adjust head that's great for both beard and mustache maintenance. The precision comb is handy for controlling length too, and there's very little tugging around the neck. And if you leave it a little too long to get your beard into shape? It holds its charge surprisingly well when tucked away in a bathroom cabinet.”

Like the Philips Norelco Multigroom models, Braun's All-in-One Trimmer Series 9 is a jack-of-all-trades option that can do far more than tidy up your beard; the box is packed with a nose and ear trimmer, a precision head, and longer guards, too. But what separates this trimmer from the rest of the pack is the built-in dial that offers 40 trim-length settings. It’s top-notch precision in minimalist packaging. I think it’s the only real contender for the top spot on this list—perhaps that price and slightly less enduring battery are its shortcomings compared to the Philips Norelco 9000, but I do find it a superior device in terms of ease and design.

Where other devices require you to swap out different heads or attachments, or ask you to pick between bigger length gaps than you’d prefer, Braun’s Series 9 offers half-millimeter increments from 0.5 to 20 without having to futz with extra accessories. In my testing, that made the trimmer the most user-friendly device on this list—no swapping guards as you fade your beard or neckline. Plus, the Series 9 is fully waterproof for those of you shaving-in-the-shower fans looking to speedrun your morning regimen. (And I’ll admit, shaving in the shower certainly makes clean-up—of both the beard hair mess and the trimmer—faster and easier.) Bottom line, Braun’s All-in-One Trimmer Series 9 is exactly what the name promises. If it seems a little expensive, that’s because a beard trimmer that can handle all these tasks, and handle them well, isn’t cheap.

Long-term testing notes: As I said above, this one has been getting lots more mileage from me lately, and I am so pleased with that fact. I absolutely adore how easy it is to navigate between the smallest minutiae of trimming lengths without swapping guard heads, and that detail shaver has been so clutch at keeping my neckline, cheeks, and beard perimeter cleaned up. My one complaint from a recent trip was that it’s quite difficult to repack everything into the carrying case, if you bring along all attachment heads. Besides that… perfect grooming tool. Adam Hurly

“Before this trimmer came into my life, I made a couple of cheap purchases. The style I like it's 1mm overall with a 2mm on my chin and 2.5 on my mustache. The problem was the other trimmers could not handle it on a daily basis. I am the type of guy whose beard grows back really fast, so I'd trim my beard. Then, the next day, you could see clear growth, and when I tried to do it again, it just wouldn't trim the same. I'd end up hurting my face a little bit. Not this trimmer. This trimmer can handle my beard on a daily basis without hurting my face. It's that good and efficient. It's built for heavy performance and durability. For the first time I am able to maintain my beard on a daily basis.”

Wahl is a pedigreed name in the professional and home grooming worlds, but that doesn’t mean it’s done innovating. Its new High Visibility trimmer has a killer app: the trimming attachment is angled so the teeth sit “above” the base, letting you get eyes on the action in the mirror as you mow through facial hair. It’s maybe not a priority if you’re just doing leisurely trims, but if you’re trying to get the perfect line at your cheek, sideburns, or neck, that little bit of offset is a godsend.

Suddenly I’m seeing very clearly exactly where the blade is hitting. If you’ve ever had to drop that cheek line too far down or do the back-and-forth thing with your burns, you’ll recognize what a game changer this is. The Wahl High Visibility trimmer’s laser-pointer precision is boosted by some of the best ergonomics in the game. The body’s relatively thin with an excellent rubber grip, which lets you hit difficult angles like a professional pool player. The High Visibility trimmer is new to the market, but I’m betting it’ll become a barber favorite—and yours, too, if you’re doing daily touch-ups to keep those lines looking sharp.

Long-term testing notes: I find myself using this more often as a detail trimmer than a full-on trimmer. I think it’s a fantastic trimmer through and through, but I pull it from the bullpen as a closer; that’s where I hold it mostly in my mind—and happily! Adam Hurly

"Absolutely amazing product. Heavy, rock-solid construction makes the hand feel confident, has great ergonomics, and has a solid grip even when the hand is soapy. But the best part is the forever blade makes it easy to see what’s getting cut, even with guard on (I used the 2). Most precise edge for a jawbone line beard I’ve ever had. And with the guard, it combs as it cuts with the grain of the hair, keeping stray whiskers knocked down. I’ve been pinched/cut before with fatter spaced blade rakes, but I didn’t feel threatened trimming under the nose."

The MultiShape lets you build a grooming kit around the things you actually use. Start with this beard and hair trimmer, then add a nose trimmer, foil shaver, or even a toothbrush head if you want them. Everything shares one rechargeable handle, which makes much more sense than finding room for another charger every time you buy a new device. Other manufacturers – take note.

This starter kit includes the lithium-ion base, beard and hair head, and two combs. The other attachments cost extra, so factor those in before deciding how much money or luggage space it’ll save. Panasonic rates the battery for 90 minutes, with a one-hour charge.

Long-term testing notes: Over several weeks, I used a broader MultiShape kit for shaving, beard maintenance, and brushing his teeth. Swapping heads was quick, and the light handle made the shared system easy to live with. The beard head coped with ordinary growth, although particularly stubborn hair exposed its limits. With daily toothbrushing and shaving three or four times a week, he charged the handle roughly every fortnight. That convenience made it a favorite for travel, while a dedicated beard trimmer remained the stronger choice for dense growth. Owen Gough

"The upside of buying a beard trimmer that can double-up as an electric toothbrush with the right attachment is you've got one tool to rule them all. The challenge? You might need a couple of passes with the trimming head to get an even finish. Compared with the more traditional alternative, it's a bulkier device with its guard fitted.”

For anyone whose morning routine involves keeping a few days’ growth under control, the dedicated Beard Trimmer 7000 keeps things pleasingly straightforward. Its adjustment dial covers 40 lengths, while the textured handle gives you something secure to hold before the first coffee has kicked in.

The dial is the main reason to choose this over a kit with a bag of fixed guards. You can adjust the length without hunting for the next comb, then use the detailing attachment to tidy the edges. It’s a more focused choice than Philips’ all-in-one kits if beard maintenance is the job you actually need done. Just don’t mistake the hair collector for a return of the old vacuum trimmer – it’s another part to empty and clean.

Long-term testing notes: I found the Series 7000 easygoing around my chin and sideburns, with little cleanup needed for stray hairs. Its reassuring weight and textured grip also helps, even if the plastic finish isn't quite on par with Philips' now-retired all-metal Series 9000. Truthfully, this trimmer did struggle a little around the awkward patch beneath my nostrils with its bulky combs making it harder to get a neat finish. I also don't bother much with the removable hair collector – I'd rather clean the sink once rather than wash another attachment. As an everyday trimmer, this is still a solid pick. Rob Leedham

“This trimmer is perfectly functional for its price, and its two-hour battery life means I'm yet to be caught short without any charge mid-shave. As much as I appreciate its efficiency, I do miss how the older metal design looked on my bathroom sink-top. This plastic iteration feels cheap (and a little flimsy) in comparison.”

No attachments; no problem. For a beard trimmer that can only do one thing (but is damn good at doing that), Manscaped's Beard Hedger will make light work out of the bushiest, burliest beards. Its zoom wheel controller lets you dial in the comb's length between .5 and 10 millimeters for even shaves, while the waterproof construction means you can shower and shave to save time on your morning or nighttime rituals. The built-in comb is great for picking up hairs that are stuck to your face so that every strand gets whacked, because few things are more unsightly than stray long hairs poking out from an otherwise well-groomed beard. Adam Hurly

“I've owned maybe 5 or 6 beard trimmers over the last 15 years. Make no mistake, this is the most expensive, but hands down it's also the best (that includes competition from Braun, Philips Norelco and Wahl). The quality is the first thing you notice as soon as you unbox it - the feel of the handle and the quality of the blade, even down to the USB charging cable which doesn't have the usual cheapness you'd expect from an accessory that's something of an afterthought.”

If you’re researching beard trimmers, you’ll see the term “zero-gap” a lot. So, what’s a zero-gap trimmer? A zero-gap trimmer cuts as close to the skin as possible, effectively a 0mm cutting length. That can make them dangerous for novices, as you can easily cut your skin or ears while you trim. But for the highest possible level of precision, that’s what you want. (The Bevel Trimmer can also be adjusted so it has a slightly longer taper.)

This trimmer was designed by Black men, for Black men, and damn does it look good. It’s a work of art that design lovers will appreciate. This sculptural device will look mighty impressive on your bathroom counter and feels phenomenal in your hand. It’s a true barber-quality trimmer, perfect for guys with curly or Afro-textured hair. It’s also one of the most powerful trimmers for home use, with a 6,000 RPM motor. Despite that, it beats all comers in terms of battery life, with an 8-hour charge that will last for months. A word of warning: This trimmer doesn’t come with any attachments or comb guards. That’s by design, as it’s a precision trimmer for making clean lines and shaping up longer beards. If you want to cut precise hair lengths, opt for the Bevel Trimmer Pro or purchase extra attachments like the T-Blade. Adam Hurly

"I’ve been cutting my own hair for years. Let me tell you these are the best trimmers I’ve ever used. Nothing on the market compares. I mean every word. The best!!!! Switch the original blade that comes with it out with the t-blade and I promise you that line up gone be crispy like bacon! Bevel with T-Blade is King!!!"

One more Philips Norelco device, for good measure and good reason: This tool is adored by both our expert source and me: I love the OneBlade for its ability to switch between trimmer, shaver, T-blade, and body groomer with aplomb. I think it's one of the best-designed tools in facial hair care right now, and a dozen other brands are releasing dupes to chase the same high.

“I appreciate how affordable it is and how easy it is to find at drugstores since so many clients ask me where to buy it because they love it too,” says DeZarate. “There was one week where I needed to buy three of the OneBlade for different clients during press events, so that they were able to actually travel home with it because they loved how easy it is to use and that it's universal. It does a really nice job at creating clean lines and is great for sensitive skin.” This one is easy to torque in different directions, too, allowing its shaving function to act like a T-blade trimmer while also offering familiar cartridge-shave movement for anyone who wants an entirely clean mug or simple a neckline tidy up. Get one with the body grooming attachment, too, and you could have an all-in-one grooming device for all facial and manscaping needs; it really does it all with that one singular blade.

Long-term testing notes: Like DeZarate, I frequently reach for this guy to mind the details; it’s an easy tag-along for any trips (especially if I need some body trimming all the while) and will certainly be with me on a big three-month trip I have to take soon; it’s a terrific head-to-toe customizer, though I don’t necessarily rely on it when I’m at home and have dedicated devices for each task. It is a terrific middle-ground pick, for the guy who wants things streamlined. Adam Hurly

“I have to admit, I’ve avoided this product for the past few years. For some reason I didn’t think it was something I needed. I recently started maintaining my beard on my own more and needed something with a bit more precision. Safety razors and straight razors were cutting up my face. My $200 electric razor cuts good, but is terrible at getting straight edges. So I figured I would give this a try and I must say I’m very happy with it. This is a very high quality product for the price. Not only does this razor provide the precision I needed to line up my beard, but it also shaves very very well.”

Vacuum trimmers keep you from having dozens of errant clippings littering the sink, but this one is more than just a vacuum—it has a detailing and edgework attachment and can trim up to 18 mm with a line-drawing detail head that rivals most T-blade trimmers.

Panasonic's wet/dry beard trimmer has a convenient wheel that lets you switch between guard lengths effortlessly—a huge boon when you're trying to shape your beard.

A display screen on your beard trimmer? In this economy? If it seems too good to be true, we get it, but this easy-adjusting trimmer from Panasonic is, in fact, the real deal.

For just 25 bucks, you can get this all-in-one trimmer from Philips that does a surprisingly good job when it comes to shaping and maintaining your scruff. Is it the fanciest trimmer on the list? No, but it works.

You want a beard trimmer that’s simple, effective, and doesn’t come with useless features or add-ons. Here are a few features to consider when looking for a great beard trimmer.

We look at how evenly a trimmer cuts, how comfortable it is to use, and whether its attachments make different jobs easier. Power matters, but so do the small frustrations that become obvious with regular use – awkward combs, difficult cleanup, or a handle that’s hard to hold. We also compare battery life, charging, and the range of cutting lengths against the price.

Adam Hurly has reviewed grooming products since 2013, and his years of testing underpin this guide. Timothy Beck Werth contributes his own hands-on findings alongside his wider coverage of grooming and consumer technology. For this update, we’ve also drawn on my reviews for British GQ, with the relevant tester and any differences between British and US kits identified in the entries. Read more about GQ and how we test and review products.

There’s no denying: The Philips Norelco Multigroom 9000 is the best beard trimmer you can buy these days. If its $100 price tag is too steep, the baby-brother Multigroom 5000 is a solid fallback. It’s not shower-proof, has a shorter warranty (five years to the 9000’s eight years), has a plastic body instead of steel, and comes with a few less attachments. But at $40, it gets the basics done nearly as well as it’s pricier sibling.

Can you use a beard trimmer to cut head hair?

Beard trimmers are not meant to be used as hair clippers, since clippers require much more power to cut through thicker patches of hair. However, some beard trimmers have the muscle to multitask, and they’ll proudly hype that skill—usually by declaring the work for “beard and head” or similar language. We usually verify those claims against product reviews, too. And frankly, we’d probably just opt to buy a dedicated hair trimmer (you can find our roundup of the best hair trimmers here), especially if you’ll be using it often.

Barbers choose tools to suit the job, from adjustable trimmers for controlling length, to detail trimmers for sharper edges. The Wahl Pro Series High Visibility is our professional pick for precision work, while the Philips Norelco Multigroom range offers broader versatility. For home use, start with your beard length and the kind of maintenance you do most often – a tool built for crisp outlines won’t necessarily include the guards you need to trim a longer beard evenly.

Which trimmer number is best for a beard?

That's going to depend on what beard style you're going with. In order to play around with trimmer numbers, we like the Braun All-in-One Trimmer Series 9 9440 for its easy-to-use adjustment wheel.

First, wash and dry your beard so you're starting off with a clean canvas. Then, decide how short or long you want to keep that bad boy. Trim against the grain of your growth, and know that the direction of growth may vary even in similar locations on the face. It's OK to make a couple of passes to ensure you get each hair because a patchy beard is a bad beard. Finally, clean up the neckline with some sharp lines so it's neat and tidy, framing the perfection that is your beautiful facial hair.

How do I maintain and clean a beard trimmer?

Switch it off and disconnect the charger before cleaning, then remove trapped hair from the blades and combs after each use. Follow the instructions for your particular model – a washable cutting head doesn’t mean the whole handle can go under the tap. The Remington Vacuum trimmer, for example, has removable washable parts, but its body should stay out of water.

Let washed components dry before putting them away. Oil the blades if the manufacturer tells you to, but don’t assume every trimmer needs it. Philips’ current Multigroom blades are designed to work without oiling. Replace a damaged or persistently blunt cutting unit with the correct part for your model.

How do I choose the right trimmer if I have sensitive skin or ingrown hairs?

Avoid “zero-gap” trimmers, which is a trimmer that cuts as close to the skin as possible, effectively a 0mm cutting length—those can mess your skin if you're prone to irritation or ingrowns. Otherwise, since you're trimming, you usually won't have to worry about irritating your skin because the blades shouldn't ever actually make contact with your face.

What’s the best way to travel with a beard trimmer—any TSA or voltage concerns?

One of the big concerns for frequent travelers—at least in the USA—is whether they're going to be able to get their beard trimmer through security and not having it buzz during transport. If this is a priority for you, look for a model with a travel lock like the Braun All-in-One Trimmer Series 9 9440, which prevents the trimmer from turning on in transit.

How do I clean a waterproof vs. non-waterproof trimmer?

Waterproof trimmers are a breeze: Just hit ‘em with the (usually included) cleaning brush, then wash them off in the sink before drying and applying some oil. Non-waterproof trimmers just skip the rinse, so you’ll have to take extra care with the brush. You can also use spray cleaners specifically designed for grooming electricals depending on your trimmer's care instructions.

What should I do if my trimmer starts pulling hair or losing power?

First, make sure you've thoroughly cleaned the trimmer. Next, make sure it's fully charged and/or has new batteries. If it's still pulling hair, it's probably time to swap the blades (plenty of companies sell refills on their site, and make sure to check the warranty to see if you qualify for a fresh set). If it's losing power, it might be time to swap the internal battery (check your warranty!) or get a new trimmer altogether. Luckily, we haven't had that issue with any of the trimmers listed above.

Emily Clark is Head of Education at Fellow Barber and a Senior Barber at Fellow’s SoHo NYC barbershop.

Melissa DeZarate is a celebrity groomer whose clients include Matt Damon, Kenan Thompson, Matt Bomer, and Taika Waititi.

#6736. The 6 Best Ellipticals Right Now, Tested and Reviewed by Fitness Experts

Your elliptical routine doesn't need to be limited to the fitness club.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF YOU'RE IN search of an effective and extra-joint-friendly way to elevate your cardio game, you're in the right place. Yup, we're talking ellipticals. These machines are often generally thought of a joint-friendly alternative to a treadmill, and in this regard they're great. You won't truly ramp up your heart rate on an elliptical, but there is solid potential for Zone 2 cardio training, depending on your fitness level.

Cardio doesn't have to be punishing on your joints or push you to your limits, and that's precisely where elliptical trainers shine. While other cardio machines like air bikes and rowing machines may push your heart rate to the max, and treadmills simulate running and walking, ellipticals offer a unique experience. They give you a chance to burn calories while being gentle on your joints and connective tissues. According to Men's Health Fitness Director, Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S, "the elliptical won't have you pushing intensity, but it's a great way to sneak a little extra motion and heart rate work into your life."

The elliptical motion provides a smooth and fluid workout, maintaining a consistent heart rate over extended periods. This makes it an excellent choice for building your aerobic system while promoting total-body blood circulation and coordination through the synchronized movement of all your limbs. The best elliptical machines operate smoothly and quietly, offer a range of resistance levels to accommodate users, and come with built-in workout programs designed to keep your training interesting and varied. Some models even allow users to adjust the stride length, which can help mimic different types of walking or running motions.

The Bowflex Max Trainer M6 is tailor-made for people ready to challenge themselves on an elliptical. Whether you're using an elliptical to supplement your cardio or improve cardiovascular health, the M9 delivers the toughest workout we've found in the world of elliptical machines.

This elliptical leaves others in the dust when it comes to a challenging workout. Its unique combo of elliptical and stepper movements creates a workout experience that got us sweating. With 16 resistance levels at your disposal, you can gradually increase the challenge, ensuring that every session remains demanding and effective.

Let's talk specifics. The variety of handlebar positions adds versatility to your workout routine, helping you maintain proper form throughout your sessions. Its black-lit LCD screen is crisp yet modestly sized, so you can see your output in real time. The absence of entertainment offerings means you can actually lock in to your training without distractions. But if you do want to watch something, a handy holder for your phone or tablet is included.

We love it for home use because it operates almost silently. This is a significant advantage, especially if you live in a shared space or prefer to work out without creating noisy distractions.

Its construction delivers on durability and longevity, making it a worthwhile investment for those committed to their home fitness journey. The combination of tech features, reliability, and the ability to provide one of the toughest elliptical workouts in the industry makes it one of the best ellipticals we've ever tried.

Whether you're looking to burn calories or improve cardiovascular health, this machine has you covered. Its versatility, customizable resistance settings, seamless app integration, and overall build quality make it an excellent choice for individuals of all fitness levels. Its wide range of workout options and adjustable resistance settings make it suitable for nearly anyone, too.

The Schwinn 490 Elliptical Machine has proven to be the most reliable elliptical machine I've had the pleasure of using. Its sturdy construction, easy one-person assembly, and whisper-quiet operation make it as easy to use day to day as it is durable over time. The machine operates almost silently, which is a welcome feature for those who want to work out without disturbing others in their household. Working out on this machine feels like low-impact running, which is just what you want.

With 13 preset workouts, this machine offers plenty of options to keep your elliptical routine exciting and challenging. Whether you prefer high-intensity interval training, steady-state cardio, or endurance workouts, you can do it all on this machine.

The Schwinn 490 has 25 resistance settings you can adjust quickly to match your desired workout intensity. Whether you're aiming for a gentle warm-up or a grueling full-body workout, you can easily fine-tune the resistance to meet your needs.

Connectivity is a major plus. It syncs seamlessly with your smartphone via Bluetooth, letting you connect with popular fitness apps like MyFitnessPal, Google Fit, Apple Health, and more, as well as its proprietary JRNY app, making it easy to track and share your progress.

This elliptical trainer is a perfect match for individuals of all fitness levels, from beginners looking to kickstart their home gym to those craving diversity in their cardio routine. If you appreciate versatility, interactive training, customization, and a compact yet robust design, the X16 is made for you.

The X16 to switch between these modes means you can diversify your workouts from one machine and add variety to your fitness routine. The customizable, auto-adjusting stride can be set anywhere from 0 to 19 inches to adapt to most users' heights and preferences to find their perfect stride.

With 26 resistance levels and the ability to decline by 5 percent or incline up to 15 percent, giving you plenty of control over the intensity of your workouts. Whether you want to embark on a gentle cardio session or a high-intensity interval training session that leaves you breathless, this elliptical can accommodate your needs.

Its user-friendly, 16-inch smart touchscreen is your gateway to tracking personal performance and enjoying an interactive workout experience. Access to personal training and on-demand workouts adds a dynamic dimension to your elliptical training regimen. Whether you prefer virtual outdoor runs or live, instructor-led classes, this elliptical offers a ton of options to keep you engaged and challenged appropriately.

With a price tag of about $2,500 and weighing 300 pounds, it's not a small investment, but the additional features make it worth every penny.

The Max Total 16 will give you a similarly intense workout as the Max Trainer M9. In fact, the experience using either Bowflex machine is very similar. The Max Total 16 and Max Trainer 9 offer the same warranty, are the same size, have the same weight capacity, and feature the same levels of resistance. So, what's the difference? This machine features a larger, crisp 16-inch touchscreen to make streaming classes and following preset workouts even more user-friendly.

The Max Total 16 is the latest in this Bowflex series. It's super compact for an elliptical-style trainer, so it's perfect for city-dwellers with smaller living spaces. At north of $2,000, it's pricier than most ellipticals we've seen and tested. This Merach elliptical is the best choice for budget-conscious individuals who want to enjoy elliptical workouts at home without breaking the bank. This elliptical machine is particularly suitable for beginners and first-timers looking to begin building a home gym repertoire. With its durable build, user-friendly features, and budget-friendly price tag, it's an excellent option for those who want a reliable and effective elliptical without the hefty price.

Despite it being a budget model, this machine offers a comfortable workout experience. Its oversized pedals and 19-inch stride length improve its accessibility, especially for larger individuals.

Staying connected is a priority, and the Merach doesn't disappoint in this regard. It seamlessly connects to your smartphone or tablet, offering access to a library of engaging workouts. We love that the machine's resistance can be automatically adjusted during certain preset programs, which simplifies the user experience. This feature also adds an interactive element to your workouts, making it feel like you have a personal trainer guiding you towards your goals.

During my time using the Merach, I was impressed by its sturdy and stable feel, particularly for a budget model. No wobbling or instability here, even when we picked up the speed and intensity.

The main highlight of the Merach is undoubtedly its price. At under $1,000 delivered, it offers exceptional value for the budget-conscious consumer. It's not the absolute cheapest option on the market, but its combination of durability, features, and affordability strikes the perfect balance between quality and cost-effectiveness.

The Sole E25 Elliptical is all about a stable ride and high-end features without breaking the bank. That's where this machine shines.

It was co-developed with physical therapists to eliminate all strain on knee, hip, and ankle joints for an even-lower-impact workout. With 20 levels of resistance, it's completely customizable, so you're guaranteed to get a great workout regardless of your fitness level. The 20-pound flywheel, 10 preset workouts, and oversized foot pedals keep every workout feeling smooth and comfortable. Plus, it also has a cooling fan, water bottle holder, and Bluetooth speakers built into the console.

At just north of $1,000 (including free shipping), this is not just one of the most durable elliptical trainers we've tested, it's also among the most affordable machines for users of all levels. We especially love the generous, and rare, lifetime frame warranty—something even most premium elliptical trainer brands don't offer.

Ellipticals are oversized machines by design, so there’s no getting around the fact that they take up a ton of space. Of course, you’ll want to ensure that the models you’re shopping for will actually fit your home gym. Keep in mind that it’s not just about the overall footprint (length and width), but whether you can comfortably use the pedals, too. Allow for at least a few feet of "buffer" in every direction, including overhead, around your new elliptical.

A longer stride length is better for taller individuals, while a shorter stride length suits shorter individuals. Large, cushioned foot pedals are preferable because they accommodate different foot sizes. Compare the measurements and specs of ellipticals you're shopping to determine if the build is right for you.

You want a machine that will stand the test of time and provide reliable performance for years to come. Look for features like a sturdy frame, a generous weight capacity, robust construction, a reputable brand, and positive customer reviews that attest to its longevity. In regards to the weight capacity, you are going to want something that has your weight covered and then some, to accommodate you clothes and any additional effort you are putting on the machine. The lowest weight capacity on this list is 275 pounds, so if that doesn't cover you, choose a model with a higher limit. You're looking for an elliptical that will go the distance with you, so it's worth investing in a reliable and durable machine.

Look for a display that's easy to read and tracks key metrics like time, distance, speed, and calories burned.

Consider how loud the machine is when in use, especially if you plan to use it in a shared living space. Reading reviews can help, but consider demoing in-store models first or finding an elliptical with a buy-back guarantee or in-home trial so you can “try before you buy.” An elliptical is a serious investment, and you want to be sure you’ll enjoy yours for years to come.

Like most cardio machines, resistance level is a critical part of your experience, increasing the effort you need to put out to move the pedals and handlebars. For most people, you'll stay somewhere in the middle of the resistance range, with lower levels good for rehabbing injuries or warming up. High levels are good if you are really looking to burn calories. Being able to control the resistance is nice, so generally the more resistance levels, the better.

Look for reputable brands with good warranties in case something goes wrong with the machine. The standard you'll see is 90 days for labor and at least three to seven years for parts. More than that is great, but anything less is unacceptable to us. You may see a few manufacturers try to get away with 30 days of labor, but don't settle for that.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to test the latest and greatest training equipment, including ellipticals. I collaborated with experts and fellow editors, including the MH Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. We have been evaluating the best elliptical machines for more than five years. Our rigorous evaluation criteria cover every aspect, from size and build quality to smart connectivity and ergonomics. And yes, we consider price too, because we believe that everyone should have access to quality cardio equipment.

"Everyone should have some sort of cardio element in their training," explains Samuel, emphasizing its benefits for everyone, regardless of budget or space constraints. (This doesn't always mean a machine of course; you can get a good cardio workout by going for a run outside or even doing drills in a yoga mat.)

If you're ready to take on joint-friendly cardio workouts at home, read on for our curated picks of the six best ellipticals that are well worth a spot in your abode now and beyond.

"Like all pieces of cardio equipment, the elliptical can help on any weight loss journey if it’s a style of cardio you enjoy and are comfortable doing repeatedly," explains Samuel.

Weight loss boils down to creating a calorie deficit, meaning burning more calories than you consume through your diet. "Any device that helps you be more active throughout your day can help you burn more calories and push you closer to that deficit," says Samuel

That includes the elliptical, although Samuel cautions that "it won’t deliver the most intense calorie burn out there, and it won’t build much muscle."

However, if you enjoy the elliptical experience more than, say, an airbike or a rower, then you’ll use it more frequently, contributing to overall calories burned. Pair it with some strength training, and you'll be on your way to a well-rounded training program to achieve your weight loss goals.

Among the many reasons someone looking to invest in their health may want to buy an elliptical is one primary advantage: It provides a low-impact workout. Which makes it an especially great option for those with joint issues, older adults, or those recovering from an injury.

For those who prefer some guidance and entertainment to stay engaged during lengthy cardio sessions, you're in luck. Many ellipticals on the market today offer a range of workout programs and modes included trainer-led sessions, live leaderboard rankings, global scenic routes, and more. Making it hard to ever get bored.

Zone 2 training is defined by working out with your heart rate hovering between 60 and 70 percent of its maximum. Think of it like this: When exercising in zone 2, you should be able to talk on the phone, but the person you're talking to should be able to tell that you're working out.

It's more than just a workout; some believe it's a key player in building and strengthening your mitochondria—the cellular powerhouses responsible for generating the energy needed for muscle contractions.

Not truly. You're getting full-body motion, but you're not getting a truly full-body workout, says Samuel. "There are too many things not happening on the elliptical that would happen if you were going out on a run or using a different cardio machine, such as a rower," he says. "You're not accelerating or forcing your body to deal with natural deceleration (as you do when you run), and there's very limited potential progressively overload (which happen when doing even basic calisthenics workouts). An elliptical can supplement a full-body workout, but it's not a replacement for one."

While treadmills and ellipticals are similar, they differ in a few key ways. Researchers found that elliptical trainers provide the same cardiovascular benefits as treadmill running, without the impact on your joints. So they're a perfect solution if you're a runner who wants to stay in race shape without excessive pounding to your ankles, knees and hips.

But a 2021 study that the treadmill burns calories at the highest rate of any exercise machine. If you're looking for a cardio machine that's easier on joints, an elliptical can be useful. However, if you want a rig that burns calories fastest, invest in a treadmill instead.
