All that to say, the ritual of gift-giving is always made to be much more meaningful when we can collect all the little, delightful items we’ve collected over the year and share them with those whom will appreciate them most. Maybe that’s a simple, but utterly practical thingamajig that has made your life that much more convenient. Or something you came across in your travels. Even an item you have at home for years that you couldn’t imagine living without. Here are a few self-care accessories that I've encountered both recently and not-so-recently that fit that bill.

Ever since the days of chewable Flintstones vitamins, we as a human race have been striving for new, inventive ways to get our daily dose in. Straight pills are boring and require water. Powders are messy and not easily transported. Gummies can be overly sugary and harden over time. But strips are nearly weightless, easy to travel with, and consumable on their own. The ones made by StripIt dissolve on your tongue, a little like a Listerine mint strip, and come in four different formulas: Vitamin C, D3 + K2, B12, Sleep, and Digest. Though they can take a little bit longer than a mint strip to dissolve, they’re still a really convenient way to make sure you’re keeping up with your supplements. I’ve been using the D3 + K2 ones while I travel. They taste pretty good and are colorful and novel enough to function as a small stocking stuffer or Hanukkah gift for the health hawk in your life.

I will never tire of a big, beautiful block of soap. Especially if it's so fragrant that it fills a whole room with its smell. My new favorite in this category is Life Research Lab, an herb-forward brand that takes inspiration from (and incorporates) the local LA flora into its soap blends. There’s the eucalyptus and grapefruit pumice slab that draws from common neighborhood trees, a classic “cowboy cologne” mix of cypress and California sagebrush so commonly found in Angelenos’ gardens, and a juniper bergamot number that lifts scents from the desert. Many of them contain bits and pieces of the very plants they’re named for, which function as light exfoliants as you scrub. I was especially charmed by the Christmas Morning Soap, which is infused with balsam fir essential oil and pinyon pine leaf. Its name, price, and the fact that it comes in both 9-ounce blocks and 4-ounce cylinders make it a perfect stocking stuffer. T’is the season.

When I traveled to Seoul a few years ago, I popped into the Hinok store and spent about 20 minutes smelling basically every one of its products, which all contain ingredients sourced by foraging detritus from old cypress forests on Jeju island (not cutting them down). Alas, I couldn’t bring anything home because my carry-on was already stuffed. But recently I learned the brand is available to buy in the US and had a chance to try a few things out. My favorite is the thick, gooey body wash. It has the consistency of honey, and emanates a light, fresh natural scent without being too overpowering. Most crucially, the formula is gentle enough to clean your body without stripping it of its natural oils. After searching for a light body wash I can use daily for a while now, this qucikly became my new favorite. (The deodorising spray is really good for households with pets too.)

When I was in New York last month, my future sister in-law suggested we take a quick field trip to Senti Senti, a little skincare store in Chinatown. To my delight, they carried imported Korean and Japanese formulas of lotions, cleansers, and—most importantly—sunscreen from popular brands like Beauty of Joseon and Bioré. (Don’t ask me how this is allowed, Chinatown’s gonna Chinatown.) In the 15 minutes we spent there, we observed at least three people walk in and beeline for this Dr. Althea face lotion and I couldn’t help but be tempted. Using it for the past month, I’ve been impressed with how light, hydrating, and easily absorbing it is—an excellent goop to apply in the morning. For anyone who hates the lingering feeling of a heavy day cream, this one’s a no-brainer.

We’re days away from the start of winter, meaning we’ll all be heating up our homes and braving, windy, sub-zero temperatures more regularly for the next few months. All of that means our skin has a far higher chance of getting dry and flaky. Enter Bein All-Over Body Oil. The blend of organic sesame seed, squalane, and camellia oil rubs on smoothly and absorbs like a dream, leaving no sticky residue behind. Body oil can be especially helpful for feet, knees, elbows, and hands, post-shower. And is light enough that you can apply lotion on afterward, too. Best of all, the San Diego-brand’s products smell faintly of bitter citrus, like a little Aperol spritz for your skin. It’s bright-red packaging makes it feel especially festive for the holidays.

A good robe, in my humble opinion, must rise to a few crucial tasks. It should be able to absorb water well, dry out quickly, and let your skin breathe after a long warm soak in the bath or shower. It should also allow you to lounge around your household without flashing your living companions or getting furniture wet. That’s why I’m partial to a long linen kimono, which checks all of those boxes. I was gifted a sophisticated blue-striped one from Deiji Studios nearly six years ago for Christmas, and it’s now a perfectly worn-in, indispensable bathroom staple. No wonder Deiji still sells it. Even better, it’s on sale for Black Friday.

#6726. Before You Shop Glossier’s Black Friday Sale, Here’s Our Ranking of the 15 Best Products

Once the new kid on the block, Glossier is one of the biggest and most well-known (and loved) makeup and skincare brands out there. “Cloud Paint” and “Boy Brow” aren’t just product names now; they’re trends that developed whole product categories, igniting the launch of a zillion dupes. It’s iconic, to say the least.

Glossier became known for its minimalist approach, both in packaging and product formula. Every makeup product is filled with skin-loving ingredients (like hyaluronic acid and glycerin), the skincare is gentle and suitable for all skin types, and their approach to beauty is simple and fresh-faced. From the best-selling Balm Dotcom to makeup artist-favorite Stretch Concealer to the hidden-gem bodycare—choosing a favorite child is hard. That’s why I ranked and reviewed all of the best Glossier products below.

While we’re here... Glossier is running its annual Black Friday sale right now. FWIW, Glossier rarely goes on sale. The brand really only does discounts during its annual Black Friday sale, meaning you won’t see prices this low for likely another year. I know 25% off doesn’t feel all that buzzy or exciting (it’s not the same shock as all those TVs and gaming consoles you stood in line for as a kid), but it’s one of the highest I’ve ever seen Glossier offer. And if you spend more than $100, your discount shoots up to 30% off. That, my friends, is a steal in the Glossier world.

Did you too pluck your eyebrows just a little (read: a lot) when you were younger? Unforch, the sentiment is v relatable, but this brow gel helps give that fluffy appearance even when you don’t have too much going on above your eyelids. “It's the only brow gel that visibly thickens my brows upon application,” editor Corinne Sullivan notes. “My favorite thing is how it keeps my brows conditioned rather than crunchy like other products do.”

When it comes to blush, Glossier’s beginner-friendly Cloud Paint will forever remain a cult-favorite pick among beauty lovers. “Sorry, but Cloud Paint is still the GOAT of all cream blushes,” beauty editor Beth Gillette shares. “Yup, I said it!!! It blends better than any other formula I've used, especially with my fingers, making it practically the simplest blush to apply ever. The shades are timeless and trendy and I'll never get tired of 'em.”

Beauty director Lauren Balsamo is obsessed with these blushes (she even said it was her favorite makeup launch last year). “The original Cloud Paint provides a nice wash of color that lasts for an hour or two, but Plush Blush lasts all day without fading, even on my extremely oily skin,” she says. “I’m not someone who wears primer or sets my makeup with a setting spray, so I fully expect most makeup to fade after a few hours, but Plush Blush survived a 12-hour office day on my cheeks.”

If dewy glasslike skin is what you’re after, dewy glasslike is what you’ll get! As the name suggests, Futuredew is the oil-serum hybrid that will make future you dewy as hell. Packed with nourishing oils and plant-based extracts, you’ll be looking as radiant as ever in no time. Wear it alone, under makeup, or as a highlighter on the high points of your face.

Makeup artist Katie Jane Hughes got me obsessed with this brow pencil, and now it’s virtually the only one I’ll use. It has a unique, straight tip (versus the usual fine, pointy one) that helps create hairlike strokes and fill in my brows with the same tool. My brows look natural and soft every time.

Glossier might not have been the first to launch a lip oil, but it made a pretty damn good one. It makes my lips look plush and glossy and hydrates like a lip treatment. The tints are extremely sheer too, so it works with basically every lip liner I pair it with.

Where skincare and makeup come to play, this foundation feels like a smooth gel cream that melts into the skin like butter. Available in 32 shades, you can build the coverage of this foundation up or keep it as minimal as you’d like. As for its ingredients, hydration is the name of the game with a mix of squalane and glycerin.

Lip Line is one of my favorite lip liners ever, and I own more than 50 (sorry, I’m a lip liner fiend). I love how easily the formula glides onto my lips, but the best part is how long it lasts. I don’t always want a stain, but I do often want a liner I don’t have to reapply right away. These stay on for hours without needing to pull it out of my bag and re-do, and they do so without drying out my lips.

As a lipstick lover, Ultralip remains a top-tier product. The main reason is the super hydrating formula that still gives a stunning color payoff. “For long-lasting color and tons of moisture, this is my go-to balm!” editor Corinne Sullivan shares. “It provides a nice, subtle tint while keeping my lips smooth and shiny (even in the winter!).”

Looking in the mirror and seeing your under-eyes creased is a top-five woe of makeup users all around. Stretch Balm concealer is flexible, lightweight, and hydrating. It covers up all the dark circles and redness you might wake up with after a long night of watching Eras Tour livestreams (I see you, I hear you, and I am you).

Let’s be real: Not all cleansers easily take off all of your makeup in one go. This gentle solution has a pH-balanced formula that actually removes your mascara and eye makeup without excess scrubbing. It’s creamy and nourishing so you don’t have to worry about your face feeling stripped and dry after.

What can we say, we’re fans of the classics! Balm Dotcom is one of the brand’s best-selling products, and for good reason. “Let the record show that Balm Dot Calm is still one of the best lip balms out there, despite having spawned hundreds of copycats since it first took over our feeds,” says commerce writer Sarah Maberry. “Old-school Glossier fans will be happy to hear they returned to the OG formula but kept the new and improved packaging. For years, I've kept a few of the birthday cake flavor on hand for an easy last-minute gift that everyone loves. I've even had friends tell me they look forward to their annual restock.”

If you wish you could bathe in Glossier You, you’ll enjoy dousing yourself in this body butter. It’s rich and decadent as it hydrates skin with shea butter and jojoba oil. I keep the chic jar on my nightstand and coat my skin with this cream before bed, and it makes my skin soft and supple (and smell amazing).

If I could lather myself in this lotion at all times, I would. As someone with oily skin, the idea of feeling sticky/greasy after lotioning is a constant fear. But this one absorbs into the skin so well while also giving off a subtle glowing finish. It literally feels like soft silk and smells so good with its orange blossom neroli complex.

A dab of this underneath my eyes is like a primer for my concealer. It immediately plumps my skin, making my under-eyes look brighter, firmer, and more awake.

#6724. The 20 Most Iconic Colognes of All Time, According to GQ in 2026

The first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece. Well, as a longtime fragrance editor, I get a similar feeling when I smell Guerlain’s iconic Vétiver scent (or, more recently, Penhaligon’s Halfeti). These fragrances smelled exceptional when they debuted, still do today, probably still will a hundred years from now. And while fragrance, like any art form, has its trends, the truly great scents (and songs) have a way of deflecting them and singing on.

All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years. To do so, I dug through the history of men’s fragrance to put together a list of some of the most iconic colognes of all time. Scents that defined an era, changed the course of perfumery, or smelled so good that folks never stopped wearing them.

Our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time. You might love some more than others, but all have earned their place in the fragrance pantheon. Here are 20 of the most popular, influential, and enduring colognes ever made, and exactly why they’ve lasted.

Is there a more classic cologne than Acqua di Parma’s Colonia? Launched in 1916, this timeless citrus is the original Italian splash, and it would be criminal not to include it on a list of this caliber. That crisp, bright citrus opening is unmistakable, but there’s so much more going on beneath the surface as it dries down, with the supporting notes weaving in and out without ever stealing the show. Herbaceous hints of lavender and rosemary add herbal hues, while earthy vetiver and patchouli mingle with the smooth warmth of sandalwood as it settles on the skin. This is one of the great daily drivers, if not the very archetype of what an everyday cologne could or should be. It’s a 10/10 blend of citrus, aromatics, and woods, and more than a century on, still smells as sophisticated as ever.

I’ve written about Guerlain Vétiver so many times, you’d think I’d have run out of ways to sing its praises. But I could go forever. Few fragrances have done more to establish vetiver as a leading note, and since its 1959 debut, this masterpiece has remained every bit as relevant and wearable. It beautifully captures vetiver’s fresher, greener side, rather than leaning into its smoky, earthy character. There’s a crispness, with bright citrus, a touch of spice, and grassy vetiver balanced by subtle tobacco and woods, like the first cool, earthy dew on a spring morning. Elegant and confident, it oozes the kind of sophistication I imagine old-school Hollywood leading men appreciating, yet it wears just as well today, whether you're suited up or simply going about your day.

Ask me to name the most influential luxury fragrance of the 21st century, and there’s a good chance I’d say Aventus (notice, I said “luxury”). I’ve seen firsthand just how many guys made their first foray into high-end fragrance with this icon, and while I now often gravitate toward some of the deeper cuts in Creed’s storied catalog, every time I wear Aventus, the compliments roll in. Since its 2010 debut, it has inspired countless imitators and the inevitable fragrance fatigue that comes with being a phenomenon, yet I don’t think it’s lost an ounce of its appeal. To me, it's the ultimate wedding fragrance, a perfect blend of bright citrus and pineapple, aromatic freshness, and rich, smoky woods that’s refined without being fussy. The defining fragrance of the 2010s? I’d make that argument any day. Aventus will always have a place on my shelf.

No. 89 is one of the great British gentlemen’s fragrances, and few colognes capture Bond-like elegance quite like it. And it tracks: Introduced in 1951, No. 89 counted James Bond creator Ian Fleming among its famous admirers, while Cary Grant and Sir Alec Guinness were reportedly devotees as well. The scent itself is traditional in the best way, a classically composed fougère with crisp, almost barbershop-like citrus and lavender freshness, subtle florals, warming spice, and a smooth, woody base of vetiver and oakmoss. Aromatic, gently spicy, and impeccably polished, it’s the olfactory equivalent of a beautifully tailored Savile Row suit. More than seven decades on, No. 89 is proof that class and character never go out of style.

Back in the ’90s, CK One was everywhere. From Wall Street execs to flannel-wearing creatives; its intoxicating freshness just captured the zeitgeist. It was also one of the first mainstream fragrances marketed as unisex. (Almost an afterthought for fragrance fans today, it was a fairly novel concept then.) And while countless fragrances have followed in its footsteps, this citrusy, green, woodsy, lightly sweet profile still more than holds up. A surprising amount is going on here, too: a bright medley of citrus and tropical fruits, a floral heart with hints of spice, and a clean, musky base of cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s an icon that helped define a generation, and it works just as well day or night, on pretty much anyone. And perhaps most impressively, after all these years, CK One still smells unmistakably like CK One.

Much like his clothing, Ralph Lauren’s original Polo fragrance has left an indelible mark on American style. Launched in 1978, the unmistakable green-bottled cologne helped define what a classic masculine fragrance could smell like: sophisticated, confident, and unapologetically aromatic. And while nearly five decades have passed, there’s still nothing quite like it. That signature pine-heavy character is front and center, surrounded by a rich blend of herb and spices with bergamot adding brightness and leather lending rugged, earthy depth. It’s bold, woody, green, and distinctly old-school, but that’s precisely its charm. It’s undergone reformulations over the years, and its assertive character won’t appeal to everyone, but there’s no denying its place in the fragrance hall of fame. Some colognes come and go, but Polo isn’t going anywhere.

When I spotted that frosted bottle in my dad’s medicine cabinet and wore it for the first time, I had no idea that this scent would spark a lifelong fragrance obsession. Armani’s 1996 icon, Acqua di Giò, has been worn by millions, referenced endlessly, and spawned countless flankers, but the original remains one of those rare mass-appeal designer colognes that have stood the test of time. Why? Because it’s just so wearable. Long before the niche fragrance boom, when designer colognes dominated department store counters, Acqua di Giò caught on like wildfire, appealing to just about every kind of guy, whether for the office or date night. At its core is a beautifully nuanced blend of citrus, fresh marine accords, and soft florals, grounded by a musky amber base. On skin, it’s breezy, clean, and subtly woody, with an oceanic quality. If you’ve never rocked it or haven’t reached for it in years, do yourself a favor and revisit this classic.

Imitation is the highest form of flattery, and so many colognes still try to smell like Cool Water. Launched in 1988, it became a full-blown phenomenon in the ’90s, and for a generation of guys, it was practically a rite of passage. Along with CK One, it was non-negotiable during my formative years, and even then, before I’d developed my own distinct taste, I knew I didn’t want to smell like everyone else. But there was something about this intoxicating green aquatic I just couldn’t resist. Its blend of lavender, mint, rosemary, and neroli nodded to classic gentleman’s fougères, but Cool Water took that aromatic DNA somewhere new—a singular scent that’s herbal and richly marine, softened by a woody, musky warmth. While it might smell dated to some, there’s no denying its place among the most iconic fragrances of all time, and I’d argue it still smells amazing on the right dude, especially on a spring or summer day.

Terre d’Hermès is (probably) my favorite designer fragrance of all time. When Jean-Claude Ellena created it back in 2006, he delivered something entirely different from the crowd-pleasing designer colognes of the day. There’s an earthiness to it that I find irresistible, a marriage of citrus, dry woods, spice, and that unmistakable flinty, mineral character that gives it so much personality. It’s sophisticated without being stuffy, with a gorgeous, almost boozy warmth that makes it feel sultry and downright sexy. I particularly love wearing it in colder weather, when those warm, woody facets really come alive, but I can reach for it almost anytime. Plenty of designer colognes are simply pleasant, but Terre d’Hermès is distinctive and endlessly wearable.

Few colognes in modern history have generated as much conversation, inspired as many memes, or become quite as zeitgeist-y as Dior Sauvage. Love it or roll your eyes at its popularity, its influence on modern men’s perfumery is undeniable. Since its debut in 2015, Sauvage has become one of the world’s bestselling fragrances, at times even claiming the number-one spot. And it’s easy to see why. That unmistakable blend of citrus, spice, and all things ambery nice is crisp and fresh, with a warm, woody drydown that’s oh so smooth. It’s a crowd-pleaser in the truest sense, versatile enough to wear just about anywhere, though I think it really shines after dark. Sauvage has since spawned an entire family of flankers, but the original EDT started it all.

You've smelled Bleu de Chanel on plenty of guys. A beautifully composed citrus-spice-wood classic, it works just as well with a navy suit as it does with a white tee and jeans. Note: When Chanel's legendary perfumer Jacques Polge introduced it in 2010, he didn't just create another handsome, crowd-pleasing cologne; he helped define the modern blue fragrance, a fresh, clean, citrusy, and woody genre that's become a mainstay. Sixteen years on, the original remains one of the most approachable and endlessly versatile colognes ever. Its bright citrus opening gives way to an aromatic blend of cool mint, warming spices, and subtle florals, all grounded by a rich, woody base with touches of earthy vetiver, patchouli, and resinous warmth. There really is only one Bleu.

This was a tough call. Ask any scent head about Tom Ford's fragrances, and they’ll surely bring up Neroli Portofino and Tobacco Vanille, both arguably just as iconic (and good) as this one. But if you polled fans on the most influential Tom Ford fragrances, I think Oud Wood would edge out the competition. Launched in 2007, it helped introduce Oud to a broader Western audience, making the traditionally intense ingredient feel approachable. It’s elegant and beautifully blended, with a smoky, almost creamy heart of oud, sandalwood, and rosewood, accented by subtle spice and the warmth of vanilla and amber. It’s heady yet easy to wear, with an addictive richness that never wears thin.

I’ve worn pretty much every Le Labo under the sun, and while my personal favorites lean toward the eucalyptus and vetiver side of the house, there’s simply no telling the story of modern perfumery without Santal 33. Love it or find it utterly overplayed, you’ve smelled it. Since its 2011 debut, it’s wafted through elevators, the backseats of cabs, countless weddings and date nights, and just about everywhere in between. More importantly, it helped bring sandalwood into the mainstream, and became a reference point for an entire genre of warm, woody fragrances. But before everyone started rocking it, Santal 33 was, and still is, a brilliant composition: creamy sandalwood, dry cedar, cardamom spice, and leathery warmth. It’s a niche legend that has suffered from its own success, yes, but give it another ten years, and don’t be surprised if the very fragrance many got tired of smelling becomes cool all over again.

If you’re remotely a scent head, chances are you dig at least one, if not several, of Parfums de Marly’s fragrances (my personal favorite is the oud-praline magic that is Haltane). But if I had to sum up the house in one word, it would be regal. It does refined, layered elegance exceptionally well, and while some folks might champion Althaïr or Castley, to my nose, the fougère-forward Layton best epitomizes the house. Launched in 2016, it’s one of the finest fougères I’ve ever smelled, rich yet airy, with classic lavender reimagined alongside crisp apple, bright citrus, cardamom, woods, and a healthy dose of vanilla. It’s practically the template for what a modern fougère aspires to be, and its enduring popularity suggests plenty of fragrance fans would agree. It doesn’t hurt that the matte blue bottle with its signature silver dome is so flauntworthy.

Few fragrances in recent times have had the same cultural impact as Baccarat Rouge 540, becoming a signature scent for everyone from socialites to fragrance obsessives. Yes, it's polarizing, and some might argue its ubiquity has stripped it of some of its magic. But it's become a modern classic for a reason, starting with the masterful nose behind it: Francis Kurkdjian, founder of his namesake maison. Launched in 2015, it's a luminous floral amber, with saffron lending spice, jasmine bringing a soft warmth, and a generous dose of amberwood creating that glowing aura. Sultry, heady, and diffusive, it's a straight-up unisex phenomenon that smells a little different on everyone who wears it, yet still announces itself before you even enter a room. Whether you're a devotee or a detractor, there's no denying it's left its mark.

It came down to Bal d’Afrique and Gypsy Water, though plenty of Byredo fragrances could have earned a spot here. But I’m the editor, and I’m going with my all-time favorite from one of the houses that helped bring niche perfumery into the mainstream. Launched in 2008, Gypsy Water was one of the first niche fragrances I ever fell for, and it holds such a special place in my heart that I still wear it regularly. There’s something almost holy about its airy blend of incense, soft woods, bright lemon, and a whisper of vanilla and amber, all coming together with that subtle yet magnetic, almost skin-scent quality Byredo does so well. Artsy, chic, and easy to love, this woody aromatic never tries too hard to make an impression yet often leaves a lasting one.

Since its 2015 debut, Xerjoff’s Naxos has achieved near-mythic status, winning over everyone from fragrance-obsessed TikTokers to yacht-owning gentlemen with decidedly expensive taste. And I get it. This is an almost impossibly well-blended composition that somehow manages to be both decadent and incredibly wearable, making it a great place to start if you’re looking to venture into niche perfumery. On paper, the combination of tobacco, aromatic lavender, fruity freshness, and a prominent honey accord sounds like it shouldn’t quite work, but man, does it ever. That rich sweetness is a defining feature, especially in the opening, before the herbal, earthy tones and a hefty dose of vanilla come together in a downright sumptuous yet crisp way. The hype may have quieted down since its social media heyday, but Naxos deserves its flowers as a modern niche standout.

Halfeti has become a signature of mine, though I’m admittedly a little late to the game, having received my first bottle as a birthday gift last year, well after it had achieved iconic status in scent circles. But better late than never, especially when a fragrance is this good. Named after a Turkish town known for its roses, it leans into a rich, heady floral style, layered with citrus, herbs, and spice. Bergamot and grapefruit lift the opening before saffron and cardamom give way to a deep base of leather, oud, cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s a lot, but it all hangs together gorgeously, creating a woody, spicy, aromatic scent that’s elegant and sexy, perfect for special occasions or date nights. But I’d happily wear it just about anywhere, including when I’m not going anywhere at all.

Musc Ravageur embodies the risk-taking spirit of niche perfumery. Launched in 2000, it helped redefine what a modern musk fragrance could be at a time when fresh, clean fragrances dominated the men’s market. More than a quarter century later, it remains a cult favorite, thanks in no small part to its warm, almost funky (in a good way) richness. It opens with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and rose, all resting on a base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. A benchmark for animalic musks, it’s an alluring, sultry, and unapologetically sensual aroma, equally suited to being a signature scent or an olfactory companion for wherever the evening leads.

Amouage has dropped so many olfactory bangers over the years that choosing just one for this list wasn't easy. The Omani house has built its reputation on rich, complex compositions that keep you coming back to sniff your pulse points, and while I could make a case for several of its fragrances, Reflection Man feels quintessentially Amouage. Launched in 2007, it’s become a luxury niche benchmark, proving that a floral-forward fragrance can be every bit as rich and sophisticated as its woody or spicy counterparts. It opens with an herbaceous blend of rosemary, berries, and orange before orris, jasmine, and ylang-ylang bring a lush, earthy depth, all grounded by a smooth base of vetiver, patchouli, and sandalwood. The result is a layered floral-woody scent that’s distinctive without being difficult to wear, and versatile enough for everything from a boardroom to a black-tie gala. Pricey, yes, but worth every spritz.

#6723. Jaime Ray Newman Thinks Season 2 of The Hunting Wives Is “Shakespearean”

Bazaar speaks with the actress in an exclusive interview to discuss the finale of The Hunting Wives season 2

In the first season of Netflix’s erotic melodrama The Hunting Wives, desire drives most, if not all, of Callie’s decisions—and indiscretions. Her unyielding loyalty to Maple Brook’s conniving diva, the formidable Margo Banks (Malin Akerman), springs from a delusional, obsessive, unrequited love—a love worth spilling blood over. This ardent personality is exactly what first attracted Jaime Ray Newman to the role.

“The first thing that struck me about Callie, when I auditioned for the part, is that she is a woman who yearns,” the actress tells Bazaar about her sharp-tongued character ahead of The Hunting Wives season two release. “This is a woman who deeply wants what she cannot have and maybe will never be able to have because of where she was born. We’re all victims of time and place. There’s so much that she wants that she cannot and may never have.”

The Hunting Wives, like Callie’s yearning, focuses mostly on Margo, the salacious wife of the richest man in town, Jed (Dermot Mulroney). Much of the first season’s conflict stems from Margo’s extramarital affairs with both 18-year-old Brad (George Ferreira) and Massachusetts transplant Sophie O’Neil (Brittany Snow). Then, the murder of a teenage girl rattles the tiny Texas town, and the gossip and backstabbing that follow are what both pushes Callie away and brings her back to Margo’s side in a triumphant, bloody ending. This valiant act revives her romance with Margo and also lands her a reality TV show, Married Justice, with her husband, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box). “Season 1 ends on a high for Callie,” Newman says. “She’s just defended her woman, and Nancy Grace told her, ‘You’re a star.’ There’s no place but up from here. Callie ends season 1, thinking, ‘The world is my oyster,’ literally.”

In season 2, The Hunting Wives supercharges its soap-operatic storytelling, with much of the tragedy circling Callie’s character, a role Newman doubled down on for these eight episodes. “I find this to be Shakespearean in many ways,” Newman says. “It’s like a Greek tragedy, high drama.” This season, Callie’s arc is defined by utter heartbreak, as she finally confronts Margot’s true, evil, manipulative side and falls in love with a newcomer to Maple Brook, Nadia (Kim Patula), Married Justice’s producer. An effective tragedy depends on someone having something substantial to lose.

Bazaar spoke with Newman about Callie’s central role in the second season of The Hunting Wives, the tragic final two episodes, and how she believes her character is gearing up for revenge in season 3. Spoilers ahead!

I’m not a reality-TV-show watcher, but when I figured out we were doing this, I did a deep dive. For the photo shoot, I probably had 50 photos of these women from the Real Housewives in my trailer: how they posed, what they did with their lips, what they did with their hands, where their breasts were. My trailer was plastered with [their photos] and also Kristi Noem. We copied Kristi’s wig, and I studied her make-up. She’s in baseball hats and tactical gear. We stole a lot of ideas from her belts. May her career rest in peace, but she was a real North Star.

Margo gives Callie the greatest gift in saying, “You’re not my person; you need to move on.” She’s very clear about that. There’s the scene when I pull up in my truck, and I realize she left my romantic dinner I made for her and went to be with Sophie. Callie is devastated by it, but very soon after, this wonderful door of Nadia opens.

Kim had a really tall order, and it’s just become a hit with all these characters that have [gotten big enough to be parodied] on SNL, for God’s sake. To come and fill those shoes and find her little corner of this universe, I give her so much credit because she didn’t push and didn’t try to overwhelm anyone. It’s a very natural reaction to come on set and feel like you have to prove yourself. Kim is such a good actress that she leaned back rather than leaned forward. She made us come to her, and you can feel that in her performance. She’s so good. Isn’t she amazing? I loved working with her. Every time there was a Callie and Nadia scene, every day was a little different. She and I would rehearse on our off days. We’d run lines together, go to the gym together, work out together. We became really good friends. I didn’t know she was going to be killed because I didn’t get all the episodes. Early on, like in season 1, we got all the episodes. We walked into season 1 knowing everything, whereas in season 2, they came out in real time. But I had a hunch that happiness doesn’t last for very long in Maple Brook. Callie’s a little too happy here. Rebecca Cutter is going to rip that from her clutches very soon.

In the bar scene when Nadia tells me that she’s gay. I remember there were a bunch of takes that we did where I could barely even say the word lesbian. It could not exit my mouth. I don’t think they used any of those takes. I don’t think Callie had ever seen someone living a life she probably would want for herself. You wanting to be an actor as a child and having a real talent and propensity for it, but your family saying, “No, you have to be a pharmacist.” You [can] go about your whole life only thinking there’s one way, in one direction, and when you’re 40, you meet someone who actually was able to do that and did have a family that was supportive, and Callie sees these parallel lives. That’s what she sees in Nadia.

I was so devastated when I saw that Nadia was killed. I couldn’t believe it because I didn’t know. How can you do that to me?! I was so upset for Callie. What’s interesting is that when I watched the whole thing—they sent it to us a couple of months ago—in the final scene where I’m shooting at the Married Justice poster, I wasn’t shooting at that in real life. Rebecca had the idea to superimpose it, and I’m shooting Margo in the head.

We played it a bunch of ways. We did it one where Callie was 100 percent certain, I’m seeking justice. She made up her mind. We shot one one-take where I’m totally conflicted, and I’m crying. Actually, we put black eye makeup on to copy Nadia. We took black eyeliner and circled my eyes, and I had black makeup tears streaming down my face. We did one where I decided, “Fuck it, I’m going to suppress everything that I know is right and I’m going with Jonny to Austin.” So I didn’t know what would end up there.

My impression from that is Callie is going to go full force for revenge. How that plays into season 3, I don’t know. But how can she not? She’s a woman who has morals and values. She was on a TV show called Married Justice! She’s not going to abandon justice now that her show’s been canceled.

Who hasn’t had a moment where you tell your partner, “I did that,” and you’re like, “Oh my God, are they still going to love me?” That’s what that moment was, because she knows those photos can unlock and really take Margo down, but it’s also showing a side of Callie that’s very unattractive. She was under a spell—in the cult of Margo, which a lot of us join. She needed to believe that she could show these photos and take the risk that Nadia might think she’s too fucking batshit. She does it to serve justice.

Before we started shooting season 1, Rebecca Cutter, our showrunner, said, “Callie and Jonny probably have the best marriage on the show. I don’t think they are beards. I think they really, really love each other, but they can’t fully fulfill each other.” Also, he’s trapped. God bless Branton. I love acting with him, and he’s really a cowboy. He’s from Texas, and he’s a full foot taller than me. It’s great casting. A relationship is about understanding. What those rules are is made up by those two people, so who am I to judge their relationship? We all enter into a pact when you commit yourself to someone else. Callie’s makes me a little sad that she could be able to live a better life without so many secrets, but these are the circumstances she was born into.

We’re all speaking in code for much of this season. We say things through daggers in our eyes that we can’t say in public. Margo has caused nothing but grief for Callie, but she can’t quit her. She can’t escape the web that this woman weaves. Who better to do it with than the magnificent Malin Akerman? Callie goes from someone who thinks that Margo is the love of her life to Margo being the devil. I don’t know about season 3, but I don’t think Callie will rest until she gets justice.

#6720. 8 Best Nose Hair Trimmers GQ's Editors Have Tested in 2026

Perhaps it never occurred to you that you might need a list of the best nose hair trimmers until this very moment. Fear not—reasonably priced, speedily shipped (thanks, Amazon), simple-to-use options populate this list of our favorites. Meaning—whenever you have a general facial hair emergency that calls for rogue hair removal, you need not add an ear hair trimmer or brow trimmer to your cart. You need only think back to this moment and thank your lucky stars for choosing a gadget to cut hair—wherever it may appear.

Similar to other battery-operated beard trimmers, back shavers, razors, hair clippers, or body hair trimmers, these trimmers are ergonomic and designed with durability in mind. You can use many of them on wet or dry hair to trim nose hair, and like other electric razors you may be familiar with, most can actually be used for nose & ears (and also as eyebrow trimmers).

If you’re looking for a quick, pain-free way to get rid of unwanted nose whiskers, Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer Series 5000 can absolutely handle that. But this versatile grooming device also covers most hair-detailing needs with precision and gusto. Add in the affordable price, and that’s why it stands as our pick for the best nose hair trimmer, bar none.

The 5000 Series includes three types of trimmers: a linear-style trimmer, plus the rotary and detail attachments. Depending on your preference, you can use either the linear or rotary trimmer for both nose and ear hairs as well as working as an eyebrow trimmer. Personally, I appreciate the size of the cylinder on the rotary trimmer, which is wider than most and is able to capture overgrown hairs better than any other trimmer I tested. The linear trimmer works great at managing eyebrows (thanks to two different guard lengths) and tending to fuzzy ear canals. Perhaps the unsung hero of the kit is the straight-edge detail trimmer, which is more than capable of daily touch-ups. Think sideburns, mustaches, or even edging beards in a pinch.

The 5000 Series is battery-powered, cordless, easy to wash with a rinse in the bathroom sink, and you already know that anything made from Philips Norelco has longevity. If what you’re after is a no-frills device to manage most facial hair needs, consider this trimmer twenty bucks well spent. Adam Hurly

True to its name, Wahl’s Micro Groomsman is easily the smallest nose hair trimmer we recommend—but don’t let its diminutive size fool you. This is a perfectly pared-down trimmer that’s great for home use, and even better for travel. Heck, it’s so small you might forget you stashed it in your dopp kit.

The Micro Groomsman offers two interchangeable heads, including a rotary trimmer for nose and ears, and a linear trimmer for detailed work. You can also attach an eyebrow guard to manage any overgrown caterpillars up top. The compact design feels great in the hand, and the stainless steel blades are cinch to clean. Even if you have a primary grooming device you love, we readily recommend the Wahl Micro Groomsman as a go-to backup option or a permanent accessory in your travel kit. Adam Hurly

Got a partner who absolutely hates when you leave trimmed hair in the sink? This one’s for you. An upgrade from the standard Panasonic ER-GN30 (shown in the video), this trimmer offers everything you’d want from a dedicated nose hair trimmer, but what sets it apart is a vacuum system that sucks up clippings in an instant. Easy clean-up, yes, but the vacuum system also helps prevent bacteria build-up. We call that a win-win.

Otherwise, this tool is fairly minimal with no fancy attachments. You get a rotary trimmer, and that’s all. Granted, it’s a powerful one that’s able to mow down the coarsest strands. All told, the GN70-K is best for the person who just needs a dependable nose and ear trimmer that will save them from the mess. Adam Hurly

A whole grooming kit is excessive if all you need to tackle is the occasional nose hair. But if you’re also maintaining a beard, tidying body hair, or cutting your own hair, Philips’ 9000 starts to make much more sense. The current kit has 23 tools and accessories, including a nose and ear head, with a stainless-steel handle and rubber grip. Philips rates it for up to six hours between charges.

Long-term testing notes: Philips' previous iteration of the Multigroom 9000 was my go-to grooming tool. Alas, I only realized how much I relied on its nose hair shaving attachment after I lost the thing. Now there's a new (albeit broadly similar) update of the same device, and I'm back to trimming as much hair as humanly possible with one device. My advice for anyone else who picks up this trimmer? Be sure to check every piece when packing up after a trip. Adam Hurly

My nose hairs have become alarmingly ambitious with age, which is unfortunate given how little enthusiasm I have for plucking, waxing, or the local Turkish barber’s fire tricks. The Weed Whacker 3.0 Pro, thankfully, gets the job done with considerably less drama. Alongside its rotary nose and ear head, there’s a separate eyebrow blade with a 2mm comb. USB-C charging saves another proprietary cable, and the travel lock stops it switching on in your bag.

Long-term testing notes: During my review testing, the rotary head cut through my thick, wiry hairs quickly, without the pulling and sneezing fits I’ve experienced with cheaper trimmers. It was still ticklish, but the compact head was easy to maneuver around my nostrils and ears. The LED helped in my dimly lit bathroom, showing hairs I might otherwise have missed. I also liked the solid-feeling matte-black handle and how easily it rinsed clean. The claimed hour of runtime held up in testing, too. It’s the best dedicated nose trimmer I’ve used. Esat Dedezade

If you have a beard and your grooming routine requires a more exacting tool, ConairMan’s Nose and Ear Trimmer kit will serve you well. I think of this more as a mustache and beard-line tidier-upper, as opposed to a nose hair trimmer.

The tool has a rotary blade that makes quick work of nostril hairs. But its two-faced trimming and shaving head is its best calling card—you get a straight-edge detailer on one side, and a shaver on the other. If you’re looking for a tool that can truly tend to the lower half of your face, ConairMan offers an excellent package that’ll get the job done. Adam Hurly

Philips’ 7000 costs less than the 9000 above and still covers far more than nose hair. The US kit includes 22 tools and accessories, with a precision comb for short facial hair and heads for wider grooming jobs. Finding somewhere to keep all those small parts is part of the deal.

My main complaint, as always, is the proprietary charging connection. The supplied cable plugs into USB-A at the other end, but you still need Philips’ cable to charge the trimmer. Braun, Remington, and other brands are just as guilty of this, by the way.

Long-term testing notes: In my three-week test of the 7000, its nose and ear attachment cut comfortably without pulling, snagging, or irritation. It was much less unpleasant than plucking. The wider kit also earned its place on my chest and underarms, so the extra attachments felt useful. Esat Dedezade

If you already have a Panasonic MultiShape, the nose-trimming head gives its rechargeable handle another job. It swaps with the system’s beard trimmer, shaver, and toothbrush heads, so there’s one less complete gadget to pack when you travel.

For a new buyer, the lithium-ion handle and nose head cost around $81.99 together. The $21.99 attachment won’t work on its own, and the other heads cost extra. That makes the MultiShape easier to justify if you’ll use more of the system. For nose hair alone, a dedicated trimmer is a simpler buy.

Long-term testing notes: During several weeks with a broader MultiShape kit, I found the nose head cleared unwanted hair without pain or friction. The lightweight handle was comfortable, and switching from trimming to shaving or brushing his teeth took little effort. That ease of moving between jobs made the system particularly useful for travel. The handle and nose head linked here are sold separately from the other attachments he used. Owen Gough

While many nose hair trimmers tout motors with serious RPMs and boast about their long battery life, the truth is, you won’t be using it much—maybe once every couple weeks for a mere 5 or 10 seconds. But that’s no excuse to skimp on them, either. Here are a few things to consider:

We’ve tested all manner of nose hair trimmers for this guide, from simple battery-powered models to grooming kits with interchangeable heads. We look at how comfortably they cut, whether they pull or miss hairs, and how easy they are to handle and clean. Extra attachments need to be useful, and we consider battery life and charging alongside performance.

The guide draws on Adam Hurly’s years of grooming reviews and Ian Burke’s experience of living with the Zorami trimmer long after receiving it as a joke gift. My additions bring in testing for British GQ, alongside Owen Gough’s assessment of the MultiShape system. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation. You can read more about our editorial standards at About GQ.

The best men’s nose hair trimmer is Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer 5000 Series, according to GQ. The powerful device offers dual trimming options (for internal and peripheral nostril hairs) and also functions as a facial hair, eyebrow, and ear hair trimmer.

Whether you are using a rotary head or a linear head, nose hair trimmers are built with a protective guard, which ensures the blade doesn’t come in direct contact with the skin. The protective guard also helps you get a clean cut so the device doesn’t pull or pluck at your nose hairs. Generally speaking, nose hair trimmers do not hurt.

Not only can nose hair trimmers be washed, but it is important to disinfect them between use, first by flushing out stray hair clippings. Let them dry before storing, too, to avoid rust and bacterial proliferation between each use. It’s a good idea to clean the device again before using it, since it is going into your nose, after all.

Do you need a nose hair trimmer, and how often should you use it?

If visible nose hairs bother you, a trimmer is a simple way to keep them tidy. There’s no fixed schedule to follow – a quick trim when hairs start showing is usually all that’s needed. Concentrate on those visible hairs around the nostril opening, rather than trying to remove everything inside. Ear hair and eyebrows can be tidied as needed, using the appropriate attachment and comb.

To trim your nose hair, simply stick the trimming tip of the device in your nostril and apply a gentle circular motion. Here are a few more tips to keep in mind, according to Simone:

The cleaning systems for nose hair trimmers vary. “Some nose hair trimmers are waterproof, so it’s easy to just rinse under water, if you are the sole user, and just let it air dry,” says Simone. If you share the device with somebody else, then it’s going to be all the more important that you disinfect between uses (ideally before and after each trim). “Make sure you have tapped out the hair trapped inside to avoid clogging,” adds Simone. “For a disinfectant, I would use a sterilizing alcohol pad or barber’s disinfectant, and just wipe the tool gently dry.”

Simone (who is professionally mononymous) is a celebrity men’s groomer. Her A-List clients include Mahershala Ali, Ramy Youssef, Jason Schwartzman, John Magaro, and Brandon Perea.

Adam Hurly has been covering men's grooming for GQ since 2016. He also writes about travel. Adam is a Sioux Falls, SD native, University of Kansas graduate, former New Yorker, and current expat in Berlin. His favorite season is Oscar Season, his favorite book is Dinner At the Homesick Restaurant, and he is a proud superfan of Survivor.

#6719. “I Don’t Care About the Pointed Foot or the High Leg”— Celia Rowlson-Hall Looks for Authenticity in Movement

The choreographer is taking on Spring Awakening’s Off-Broadway Revival

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

One evening in November, Celia Rowlson-Hall slipped into a conference room for a rare break. The choreographer has spent the past four weeks rehearsing a new Off-Broadway revival of Spring Awakening, directed by Tony winner Danya Taymor, and it’s the second day of tech week. She had been holed up in Studio Seaview’s adjacent theater, fine-tuning “The Bitch of Living,” an angsty number about wet dreams, busty piano teachers, and Nietzsche. Previews were set to begin in a little over a week, and Rowlson-Hall eagerly tucked into a takeout grain bowl, fueling up for her evening ahead.

Set in 19th-century Germany, Spring Awakening is about the turmoil of developing sexuality in teenagers in a society attempting to keep them in ignorance. In 2006, the playwright Steven Sater and the musician Duncan Sheik adapted it into a musical that won eight Tony Awards, including for choreographer Bill T. Jones, who translated rebellion and repression into a gestural vocabulary. That original production also launched a generation of musical theater stars, including Jonathan Groff, Lea Michele, and John Gallagher Jr. In this spirit, the production held an open audition that attracted 2,532 performers (two actors were cast from this process). Rowlson-Hall kept her eye out for those actors with a sense of grounded earthiness and truthful storytelling. “I’m always going to be looking out for authenticity and personality inside of movement,” she says. “I don't care about the pointed foot or the high leg; it's never interested me, even as a dancer. I've never understood dance for dance’s sake.”

Spring Awakening will mark Rowlson-Hall’s theatrical debut after nearly two decades of directing and choreographing for screen. Among her work are the scenes of ecstatic prayer in The Testament of Ann Lee and Aftersun’s devastating rave sequence (she also played the adult version of the lead character). Humorously, she recently appeared in The Drama as a dance teacher intent on perfection, a mentality that couldn’t be farther from Rowlson-Hall’s own intuitive and empathetic style.

With big blue eyes and a choppy mop of dark hair, Rowlson-Hall, 42, is expressive even when sequestered behind a conference room desk. She frequently puts her fork down to gesture, including when recalling a friend’s suggestion “that all artists have one or two rocks that they will turn over their entire lives.” Rolling a pair of invisible stones around in her palms, she names religion and femininity as her thematic preoccupations. “The impact of religion in the body, specifically the female body, and what femininity looks like as taught to me by my parents versus from society and my own experiences.” She laughs, adding, “As my other friend said, ‘Celia loves a repression era.’”

Like the characters in Spring Awakening, Rowlson-Hall grew up in a small, religious community. In her case, it was Urbanna, Virginia, population 492 as of 2020, in a Christian Scientist household. She started dancing at 5 and knew from a young age that she wanted to use movement to tell stories of her own. After studying at the North Carolina School of the Arts, Rowlson-Hall moved to New York in 2006, the same year Spring Awakening premiered. “I remember hearing about the show, but also being too poor to go,” she says.

Two years later, she was planning to start her own dance company when she was asked to choreograph a music video for MGMT. She immediately felt at home on a film set, and also appreciated that the medium offered a more enduring result than a concert dancen ephemeral live performance. “The forever part,” she says. “I needed it then in my life.” She continued working on music videos, commercials, and television, absorbing lessons on filmmaking along the way. After a series of movement-based feminist shorts, Rowlson-Hall used Kickstarter to finance her first feature, Ma (2015), in which she stars in the dialogue-free dance film as a modern-day Virgin Mary on a pilgrimage to Las Vegas.

Rowlson-Hall met her now-wife, director and showrunner Mia Lidofsky, while choreographing Girls’ acclaimed “Beach House” episode in 2013. Rowlson-Hall was in a heterosexual marriage at the time, and she describes coming out at 30 as “this incredible aha moment.” But then, “Shame came in and clamped me down. I stopped moving.” It was a confusing contrast: while experiencing a profound sense of freedom and selfhood, she became disconnected from her body for the first time. Rowlson-Hall is anxious to elaborate. “The impact of me coming out was very difficult on my family, they initially had a hard time accepting it,” she says. “Then my mom got very ill, and I put my life and body on pause because I was so scared for her.” From there followed a decade of extreme highs (falling in love, marriage, motherhood) and lows (divorce, several deaths including both parents). “There were a lot of roadblocks for me to be able to find physicality and movement again because I kept getting knocked down,” she says.

She credits Ann Lee with allowing her to feel that connection again. The writer and director, Mona Fastvold, is a close friend; the two met back in the day on Gossip Girl. Rowlson-Hall was eager to inhabit the 18th century visionary, an illiterate blacksmith's daughter who became the founder and leader of the Shakers. “As a kid, I used to love to pray, it was my favorite thing,” she says. “I really wanted to ask myself ‘what if I got to decide what prayer looks like?’” She could also relate to the Shakers’ use of dance as transcendence. “From when I was young, I always felt like I was needing to exorcise things out of my body that weren't mine,” Rowlson-Hall says. “So much of what I do is trying to clear out to actually understand who I am.” The viscera is not strictly a metaphor. “When I feel like I'm going to vomit, I know that I've tapped into the right thing,” she says. “I choreograph from there, and then I can't touch it again.” She makes a gagging sound. “And then it's out of my body.”

Rowlson-Hall returned to the stage last year with Sissy, a semi-autobiographical dance-theater piece reimagining the myth of Sisyphus as the struggles of a female artist tasked with caring for a young child and an ill father. “There's something about theater and motherhood that feel very aligned,” she says with a laugh. “It's all alive and happening in front of you, and you've got to love it and let it go. It journeys on without you, you actually have no control.” That said, she’s working on her next film, which she describes as “a time traveling love story of Eve and Lilith exiting the Garden of Eden” and spending lifetimes together and apart. “There they are again,” Rowlson-Hall says. “Those old stones.”

#6718. This Jewelry Designer Bride Created Her Own Vintage-Inspired Dress for Her Polish Countryside Wedding

When the Polish jewelry designer Natalia Kopiszka was planning her August 2026 wedding to actor Aleksander “Olek” Kaleta, she found herself at a bridal fashion crossroads, stuck between two stylistic pillars of her own brand: vintage and modern.

First, the Warsaw-based designer of Kopi traveled to Paris to shop for a vintage wedding dress, but returned home empty-handed. “I didn’t find anything that I liked, so I thought: I will design my own wedding dress,” Natalia says.

For the body of her ceremony dress, she ordered fabric—silk taffeta—from Etsy. “I was on a mission to find the absolute dream silk fabric,” she says. “I started by checking out local fabric shops and silk wholesalers, but I just couldn't find the right silk taffeta with that delicate, subtle sheen anywhere.” She searched online and stumbled upon a listing from a New York-based seller, which she ordered on the spot. Luckily, “it turned out to be even more breathtaking in person than in the photos,” she says.

Then, on a weekend trip to Amsterdam with a friend, she wandered into a vintage store where she found antique lace, which she used for the bodice detailing. “The lace is truly unique because it dates back to the early 20th century, and I only had a tiny piece of it—which happened to be just enough to trim the bodice,” Natalia says. “It was such a special way to check off the ‘something old’ tradition.” She sketched the dress, then shared her designs with a dressmaker who sewed it, making her vintage-modern dream a reality.

Natalia and Olek first met in February 2021 at a house party in Warsaw. “For me, it was love at first sight,” Natalia recalls. “A friend of mine who lived in the apartment below me threw a get-together, and her roommate happened to be friends with Olek. As soon as he walked in, we instantly locked eyes. I’m pretty sure he was the one who came over and started the conversation first,” she adds. “It also turned out that Olek lived directly across the street from my apartment, so we used to wave at each other from our windows. Ever since that night, we started seeing each other almost every single day.”

After a year, they moved in together in Warsaw. In 2024, Olek proposed to Natalia during a trip to Italy, in the coastal town of Polignano a Mare. “It was a warm, romantic evening with a huge moon, and surprisingly, I didn't see it coming at all,” Natalia says. “It turned out to be such a sweet, funny moment because neither of us could stop laughing.”

On August 8, 2026, the couple held their wedding at Pałac Pstrokonie, a historic 19th-century palace in a small village outside of Warsaw. They worked with the wedding planner Kasia Fastyn, who brought Natalia’s vision—a romantic, whimsical wonderland of sorts—to life, pairing them with the event studio MyBigDay, who designed the florals and draped their dancing tent in pink fabric.

As a jewelry and accessories designer, Natalia zeroed in on all the details of her wedding looks from the beginning. She knew she didn’t want a traditional floral bouquet, for example, so she opted for a small silk bag in the shape of a bouquet from the New York-based designer Camille Albertine, after finding her work on Instagram. Albertine custom-made Natalia’s bouquet purse in the same fabric as her dress. “Everyone was so surprised that I didn’t have a typical bouquet,” Natalia says. “It’s versatile enough that I can wear it with everyday outfits. It’s going to stay with me for a long time, and I’ll even be able to pass it down through generations.”

For her reception look, the bride changed into a dress by the Polish designer Magda Butrym, pairing it with an unexpected accessory: a crochet veil cap that her sister made. “It was a really simple dress, also silk, but I put something really crazy on my head,” Natalia says.

Natalia incorporated her own jewelry into the crochet cap-like veil, which was bedazzled with charms and pendants. “They are specially made charms with little lobster clasps so you can clip them onto the crochet work however you like. They’re gold-plated and feature Swarovski crystals,” Natalia says. (Charms are a signature of Natalia’s brand, she explains, so it was only fitting to work them into her bridal looks.) Her love of historical pieces, particularly from the Victorian era, inspired the final design, which included blue stones for her “something blue.” A look inspired by it is now for sale as part of Kopi’s “I Do” bridal line.

The bride also made Olek a pocket square with the same vintage lace as her dress, so they were matching (and so he had “something old” as well). They completed their looks with wedding bands that Natalia designed. “Mine has a retro feel, crafted in gold and set with 12 small diamonds,” she says of the rings. “Olek went for a classic look—a simple, wide gold band with my nickname engraved on the inside.” Reflecting on the wedding months later, Natalia says: “Everything was perfect.”

#6712. Kim and Khloé Kardashian’s Beauty Trip Didn’t Quite Go to Plan—Here’s What to Know Before Booking Yours

Between the salmon sperm facials, the skin boosters, and the next generation of lasers, there’s plenty to pique the interest of the beauty obsessive in South Korea. So much so that vacations are increasingly being organized around visits to the dermatologist’s office. But how much is too much when it comes to our beauty itineraries? Just ask Khloé and Kim Kardashian.

On Wednesday’s episode of her podcast, Khloé in Wonder Land, Koko and her close friend La La Anthony reminisced about their August 2025 trip to South Korea, where they enthusiastically availed themselves of the country’s advanced cosmetic treatments—with some less-than-desirable results.

“Kim and I came back deformed, you came back beautiful and the plane ride just made it so much worse,” Kardashian told Anthony, recalling how their post-treatment appearances had kept them holed up in their hotel room.

The Kardashians are, of course, well-versed in the world of aesthetics. Over the years, the sisters have been particularly candid about their experiments with everything from the vampire facial to regenerative skin treatments. But even for those with the world’s most sought-after dermatologists on speed dial, things don’t always go to plan.

While it’s unclear precisely which procedures the sisters underwent—photos shared on Kim’s Instagram at the time showed her receiving facial treatments and an IV infusion—their experience raises some pertinent questions. How much research should we be doing before traveling abroad for cosmetic treatments? How many procedures can we feasibly—and safely—fit into a vacation? And how do we know when something has actually gone wrong?

The lure of a beauty vacation is understandable. South Korea, in particular, is at the forefront of aesthetic innovation, with technologies and treatments that aren’t yet widely available in the United States. And as our collective beauty literacy has expanded, so too has our appetite for more technologically sophisticated treatments. A facial no longer necessarily means an hour of extractions and massage. But there is a distinction to be made between a beauty treatment and a medical procedure. Just because something is marketed as minimally invasive, or requires no incisions, doesn’t mean it is without risk. Nor does its ubiquity on TikTok necessarily speak to its suitability for your own skin.

“Traveling for treatment isn't the same as having unsafe treatment,” says consultant dermatologist Dr. Sidra Khan. “What travel adds is complexity: a different regulatory system, possibly a language barrier, often a compressed consultation, and being thousands of miles from your practitioner during recovery.”

“A beautiful clinic, an impressive Instagram following and a gallery of celebrity clients don’t really tell you much about the practitioner’s medical credentials or what results you might expect,” adds cosmetic surgeon and aesthetics specialist Dr. Paul Banwell. Independently verify your practitioner’s qualifications and registration with the relevant medical regulator, and establish whether the clinic is equipped to manage complications. Khan recommends arranging a virtual consultation with the treating doctor before booking anything, and asking about their experience with your particular skin tone, the products and devices they intend to use, and why. “A holiday itinerary shouldn't replace informed consent.”

For London-based aesthetics and NHS doctor Dr. Alicia Gonzalez-Fernandez, the marketing of medical procedures as vacation packages is itself a red flag. “On a handful of occasions, I have encountered patients that have come into A&E straight from the airport,” she says of her experiences working in emergency medicine. She cautions against practitioners who pressure patients into additional procedures or fail to adequately discuss complications and aftercare. “We are not in the business of making people self-conscious about things that are not a problem for them.”

Then there’s the phenomenon of “treatment stacking.” While certain procedures can complement one another, squeezing several into a short period of time can increase the likelihood of complications. “Many of these treatments work by creating a controlled injury that the skin then repairs, and doing several close together doesn't give it time to recover,” explains aesthetics doctor Dr. Priya Verma. “That raises the risk of prolonged inflammation, infection and pigmentation changes, particularly in darker skin tones.”

Multiple procedures can also make it harder to establish which treatment is responsible for an adverse reaction, notes aesthetics doctor Dr. Ahmed El Muntasar. “Ultimately, I’d much rather a patient’s treatment schedule was dictated by how their skin is recovering than by the date of their flight home.”

Consider, too, how conducive the rest of your vacation itinerary is to your skin’s recovery. As Verma notes, the low humidity in airplane cabins can exacerbate dryness and sensitivity in already compromised skin, while sun exposure can increase the risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. There is no universal rule about how soon you can fly after a non-surgical cosmetic procedure, says Khan, but you should allow ample time for recovery and an in-person review before your departure. (With surgical procedures, flying also carries an increased risk of blood clots, making a conversation with your surgeon about your travel plans particularly important.)

There's also the question of downtime. An unfortunate-looking reflection in the hotel bathroom mirror doesn’t necessarily mean a treatment has been “botched.” Verma makes an important distinction: “Downtime is the expected redness, swelling or flaking that settles over a few days. Dissatisfaction is when the skin has healed but you're not happy with the result. A complication is a medical problem that needs treating.”

Knowing what to expect—and for how long—is something to establish with your practitioner well before the treatment itself. The trajectory of your recovery is key: Increasing pain, spreading redness, heat, discharge, or fever warrant prompt medical attention.

There are, however, symptoms that warrant immediate medical attention. Following dermal filler injections, for example, the FDA advises seeking immediate medical care for unusual pain, changes to your vision, white, gray, or blue discoloration around the injection site, or signs of a stroke. These may indicate that the blood supply has been compromised.

“If there are red-flag symptoms, don't just get on a plane because you'd rather deal with it at home,” stresses Khan. “Some complications are time-critical, so get seen locally.”

In non-emergency situations, contact your original practitioner for an in-person review and document your recovery with photographs taken in consistent lighting. El Muntasar recommends obtaining your full treatment records, including the names, quantities, and batch numbers of any injectables, or the device and settings used for laser treatments. Seek an independent medical opinion from someone experienced in managing complications if you remain concerned.

As distressing as it can be to feel unhappy with your appearance, resist the temptation to immediately book another aesthetic procedure. “Swelling can make certain areas appear overfilled or disproportionate, and adding more filler to try to balance things out can leave a patient with an entirely different problem once that swelling subsides,” explains Banwell.

“More treatment isn’t always the antidote to treatment,” says Khan. Anti-wrinkle injections can take around two weeks to reach their full effect, filler can take several weeks to settle, and collagen remodeling following laser treatments or microneedling continues for months. The same caution applies to overzealous at-home skincare. “Your freshly lasered face is not the moment to try the acids and retinoids you picked up at duty-free.”

And while you might have meticulously mapped out your Seoul shopping itinerary, restaurant reservations, and dermatology appointments, have you given quite as much thought to what happens when you get home? Establishing a plan for follow-up care, obtaining a record of your procedures, and checking whether your insurance covers complications should all factor into the planning process. El Muntasar recommends getting your aftercare plan in writing, including details of who you can contact outside of clinic hours and who is responsible for any additional medical expenses should you need to extend your stay.

By all means, indulge your K-beauty curiosity. Just make sure you’re approaching your dermatological appointments with a little more discernment than your haul at Olive Young.

#6708. The Art of Being Veruschka: Fashion Pays Tribute to a Legend

“There is and will always be only one Veruschka,” Richard Avedon wrote in the May 1972 issue of Vogue in an impassioned tribute to his muse. More than half a century later, his words still ring true. Since news broke of the German supermodel’s death at the age of 87, generations of fashion’s image-makers, designers, and models have been reflecting on her immeasurable influence.

A protagonist of some of the most fantastical fashion editorials ever committed to the pages of Vogue and a prolific cover star, Veruschka helped expand the possibilities of what a model could be. Her body was her artistic medium, her imagination as instrumental to the making of a photograph as that of the person behind the lens. Her creative curiosity would endure long after her heyday in the 1960s and ’70s, finding expression in her experiments with body painting and camouflage, her performance art, and her occasional, much-feted returns to the runway.

For those who knew and worked with Veruschka, though, there was as much to marvel at away from the camera: her generosity of spirit, quiet eccentricities, intellectual curiosity, and her sense of humor. In the tributes shared with Vogue below, fellow models recall their first encounters with a woman whose photographs once adorned their bedroom walls, while designers and photographers reflect on the creative communion they shared with her—and how rare a model like Veruschka is today.

I am so sad to hear the news of Veruschka’s passing. When I started modeling in 1966, she was one of my idols—she was so beautiful and exotic. I had always wanted to meet her, and then in the 1980s, while I was appearing on Broadway in the musical My One and Only, a knock came on my dressing room door after the performance. I opened it and, to my surprise and huge delight, Veruschka was standing there. It was so lovely to finally meet her, and she was absolutely divine, and we chatted for ages. She certainly is one of the greatest of all models. RIP, beautiful lady.

Veruschka was an extraordinary artist that I was blessed to know. Thank you, Vera…

I remember sitting in the library at Saint Martins, transfixed by the camouflage photographs in Veruschka: Trans-Figurations, the book she made with Holger Trülzsch. Years later, when I had the chance to work with her, I knew I wanted her to close my spring/summer 2011 show. We flew her in from Berlin and made her a bespoke dress for the finale. What I loved about working with her was how open she was to the ideas behind the collection and how wholeheartedly she embraced them. She was 71 and absolutely majestic on the runway. She had a presence unlike anyone else. A creative powerhouse and a true original.

Being a model is an art form, and she was one of the people who truly mastered it. She had both creativity and respect for what she was doing. When we worked with her, she was incredibly impressive. There was an energy, a grace, and a lasting presence that you don’t see so often today. The lifespan of a model’s career seems to have become so much shorter. I sometimes wonder if, in the way the industry works today, we’re leaving less room for someone to become truly iconic.

When I was a young girl, my bedroom walls were covered in photographs of Veruschka. To me, she looked like she had stepped out of another world—a dream I looked up to, one of the incredible women who had paved the way before me. I used to lie in bed, staring at those pictures, wondering what it would be like actually to know someone like her. Years later, that dream literally knocked on my door.

We ended up living together at our agent Zoli’s house on East 63rd Street. For months, after a long day’s work, we would settle in for the evening with our sketchbooks. I can still see her drawing her little cats—curled up, stretching out, or peeking from the corners of the pages—while I sketched beside her. We didn’t need to say much; the quiet between us always felt so full.

Veruschka was always an enigma to me, a woman with a poetic soul and a nature I could never quite put a name to. She had a wicked little smile and a twinkle in her eye when she’d look up from her drawing, as if she knew a secret about the world she might someday share. Her voice was low and sensuous, and she was always kinder than anyone needed to be.

Sometimes, while watching her sketch, I would think back to that little girl staring at the pictures on her wall. I wished I could tell her that one day she would be sitting right beside her icon, and that Veruschka would be her friend. I have always loved Veruschka, and I always will. Knowing she taught me that dreams really do come true. She was mine.

Verushka was really the first super supermodel, she was literally larger than life. I grew up with her images and like every other girl I wanted to be and look like her.

She influenced fashion in an enormous way by having that statuesque beauty but also being an incredible performer, She was not afraid of breaking boundaries creating new visions with other artists like especially all the body paint images which are now more than ever a great inspiration. May she rest in peace.

#6707. We Tried 6 Store-Bought Pumpkin Pies—These Are The Only 2 Worth Serving At Thanksgiving

A handful of things are non-negotiable at Thanksgiving. You need turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and, of course, a slice of pie to round out your meal. And pumpkin pie is the undeniable star of the dessert table.

But sometimes you're strapped for time and have too much on your plate (pun intended) to whip something up from scratch. So we tried six different grocery store pumpkin pies to find the best store-bought shortcut. And our team's verdict was pretty unanimous, even if it’s a bit hard to hear: No premade pie will ever taste as good as a homemade one.

It primarily comes down to the crust. Frozen and pre-baked pies typically rely on vegetable-based fat instead of butter because they’re more affordable, reliable, and shelf-stable—but that comes at a cost. You not only miss out on the decadent, buttery taste, but the crusts can also leave an unpleasant film on your tongue.

That said, when you need to outsource to the grocery store, we found two options that will work in a pinch.

The pie that we’d feel most confident bringing to Thanksgiving dinner comes straight from the Whole Foods bakery department. That’s not to say it’s perfect, though. The crust is almost upsettingly pale, but it’s made with real butter and only a little bit of palm oil. And since it doesn’t leave a noticeable film and still lets the butter flavor shine, we’ll let this one slide.

Once you look past the crust’s color, this pie is solid overall. The filling is decadent, not too sweet, and creamy without being mushy. Whole Foods doesn’t shy away from the spices, either.

Senior Editor Samantha MacAvoy noted that the warming spices are nicely balanced, while Designer Alison Dominguez said, “The flavor was exactly how a pumpkin pie should taste.”

Costco’s pumpkin pie isn’t perfect: The crust uses palm oil-based shortening rather than butter and can develop a soggy bottom if you buy it too far in advance. (And it doesn’t hold a candle to the warehouse’s holy grail pumpkin cheesecake.) But it has a cult following for a reason, and not just because of its $5.99 price tag.

Even with its faults, the crust has great flavor and enough salt to create a balanced bite. Dominguez appreciated how it was “flaky and not too thick, and most importantly, it let the pie filling itself shine.” News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas chose Costco’s pie as her number one pick. “It all seemed to melt together in one creamy bite,” she said.

And at over three pounds, this dessert is the indisputable champion if you want to feed a crowd for less.
